flags.taylor: Aristotle here alludes to the second book of his Last Analytics
flags.why: Taylor's note is right: the puzzle is stated in the Posterior Analytics (II.6, 92a29-33), why the definition is one; Taylor's "Last Analytics" is the old English name of the Posterior. Book Η (VIII.6) gives the full answer: the genus is as matter and the differentia as form, so that the two are one as potency and actuality are.

paragraphs.modern: We must look first at definitions reached by division. There is nothing else in the definition but the first genus, as it is called, and the differentiae. The other genera are the first genus together with the differentiae taken with it: for instance, the first is "animal", the next "two-footed animal", and again "two-footed featherless animal"; and likewise if it is said through more terms. In general it makes no difference whether it is said through many or through few, and so neither whether through few or through two; and of the two, one is the differentia and the other the genus, as in "two-footed animal" "animal" is the genus and the other the differentia. If, then, the genus simply is not apart from the species of the genus, or if it is, but is as matter (for the voice is genus and matter, and the differentiae make the species, the letters, out of it), it is plain that the definition is the account made of the differentiae.
paragraphs.greek: δεῖ δὲ ἐπισκοπεῖν πρῶτον περὶ τῶν κατὰ τὰς διαιρέσεις ὁρισμῶν. οὐδὲν γὰρ ἕτερόν ἐστιν ἐν τῷ ὁρισμῷ πλὴν τὸ πρῶτον λεγόμενον γένος καὶ αἱ διαφοραί· τὰ δʼ ἄλλα γένη ἐστὶ τό τε πρῶτον καὶ μετὰ τούτου αἱ συλλαμβανόμεναι διαφοραί, οἷον τὸ πρῶτον ζῷον, τὸ δὲ ἐχόμενον ζῷον δίπουν, καὶ πάλιν ζῷον δίπουν ἄπτερον· ὁμοίως δὲ κἂν διὰ πλειόνων λέγηται. ὅλως δʼ οὐδὲν διαφέρει διὰ πολλῶν ἢ διʼ ὀλίγων λέγεσθαι, ὥστʼ οὐδὲ διʼ ὀλίγων ἢ διὰ δυοῖν· τοῖν δυοῖν δὲ τὸ μὲν διαφορὰ τὸ δὲ γένος, οἷον τοῦ ζῷον δίπουν τὸ μὲν ζῷον γένος διαφορὰ δὲ θάτερον. εἰ οὖν τὸ γένος ἁπλῶς μὴ ἔστι παρὰ τὰ ὡς γένους εἴδη, ἢ εἰ ἔστι μὲν ὡς ὕλη δʼ ἐστίν (ἡ μὲν γὰρ φωνὴ γένος καὶ ὕλη, αἱ δὲ διαφοραὶ τὰ εἴδη καὶ τὰ στοιχεῖα ἐκ ταύτης ποιοῦσιν), φανερὸν ὅτι ὁ ὁρισμός ἐστιν ὁ ἐκ τῶν διαφορῶν λόγος.
notes: Division (διαίρεσις) is the method of Plato's Sophist and Statesman, which cut a kind into two again and again until the thing sought is reached. Aristotle keeps it, on condition that each cut is made by a differentia of the last differentia.

paragraphs.modern: But one must also divide by the differentia of the differentia. For instance, "footed" is a differentia of animal; next, the differentia of footed animal must be of it as footed. So one must not say that of the footed, one kind is feathered and another featherless, if one is to speak well (one will do this through inability), but rather that one kind is cloven-footed and the other not: for these are differentiae of the foot, since cloven-footedness is a kind of footedness. And in this way one always wants to go on until one comes to what has no differences. Then there will be as many kinds of foot as there are differentiae, and the footed animals will be equal in number to the differentiae. If this is so, it is plain that the last differentia will be the substance of the thing and its definition, since one must not say the same things several times in definitions: that is superfluous. Yet it does happen: when one says "footed two-footed animal", one has said nothing but "animal having feet, having two feet"; and if one divides this by its proper division, one will say it several times, as many times as there are differentiae.
paragraphs.greek: ἀλλὰ μὴν καὶ δεῖ γε διαιρεῖσθαι τῇ τῆς διαφορᾶς διαφορᾷ, οἷον ζῴου διαφορὰ τὸ ὑπόπουν· πάλιν τοῦ ζῴου τοῦ ὑπόποδος τὴν διαφορὰν δεῖ εἶναι ᾗ ὑπόπουν, ὥστʼ οὐ λεκτέον τοῦ ὑπόποδος τὸ μὲν πτερωτὸν τὸ δὲ ἄπτερον, ἐάνπερ λέγῃ καλῶς (ἀλλὰ διὰ τὸ ἀδυνατεῖν ποιήσει τοῦτο), ἀλλʼ ἢ τὸ μὲν σχιζόπουν τὸ δʼ ἄσχιστον· αὗται γὰρ διαφοραὶ ποδός· ἡ γὰρ σχιζοποδία ποδότης τις. καὶ οὕτως ἀεὶ βούλεται βαδίζειν ἕως ἂν ἔλθῃ εἰς τὰ ἀδιάφορα· τότε δʼ ἔσονται τοσαῦτα εἴδη ποδὸς ὅσαιπερ αἱ διαφοραί, καὶ τὰ ὑπόποδα ζῷα ἴσα ταῖς διαφοραῖς. εἰ δὴ ταῦτα οὕτως ἔχει, φανερὸν ὅτι ἡ τελευταία διαφορὰ ἡ οὐσία τοῦ πράγματος ἔσται καὶ ὁ ὁρισμός, εἴπερ μὴ δεῖ πολλάκις ταὐτὰ λέγειν ἐν τοῖς ὅροις· περίεργον γάρ. συμβαίνει δέ γε τοῦτο· ὅταν γὰρ εἴπῃ ζῷον ὑπόπουν δίπουν, οὐδὲν ἄλλο εἴρηκεν ἢ ζῷον πόδας ἔχον, δύο πόδας ἔχον· κἂν τοῦτο διαιρῇ τῇ οἰκείᾳ διαιρέσει, πλεονάκις ἐρεῖ καὶ ἰσάκις ταῖς διαφοραῖς.

flags.taylor: we say it through incapacity
flags.why: Ross's words are right: to cut the footed into feathered and featherless is a cut by an accident of the footed, not by a differentia of the foot, and comes from not being able to find the right one. Plato's Statesman (262a-263e) gives the same warning against cutting a kind into a part and "all the rest".

paragraphs.modern: If, then, a differentia of the differentia is taken each time, the last one will be the form and the substance. But if one divides by accidents, for instance if one divided the footed into the pale and the dark, there will be as many as there are cuts. So it is plain that the definition is the account made of the differentiae, and, if it is right, of the last of these. This would be clear if one changed the order of such definitions, as that of man, saying "two-footed footed animal": "footed" is superfluous when "two-footed" has been said. But there is no order in the substance: how are we to think of one part as posterior and the other as prior? About definitions by division, then, let this be enough said for a first account of what kind they are.
paragraphs.greek: ἐὰν μὲν δὴ διαφορᾶς διαφορὰ γίγνηται, μία ἔσται ἡ τελευταία τὸ εἶδος καὶ ἡ οὐσία· ἐὰν δὲ κατὰ συμβεβηκός, οἷον εἰ διαιροῖ τοῦ ὑπόποδος τὸ μὲν λευκὸν τὸ δὲ μέλαν, τοσαῦται ὅσαι ἂν αἱ τομαὶ ὦσιν. ὥστε φανερὸν ὅτι ὁ ὁρισμὸς λόγος ἐστὶν ὁ ἐκ τῶν διαφορῶν, καὶ τούτων τῆς τελευταίας κατά γε τὸ ὀρθόν. δῆλον δʼ ἂν εἴη, εἴ τις μετατάξειε τοὺς τοιούτους ὁρισμούς, οἷον τὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου, λέγων ζῷον δίπουν ὑπόπουν· περίεργον γὰρ τὸ ὑπόπουν εἰρημένου τοῦ δίποδος. τάξις δʼ οὐκ ἔστιν ἐν τῇ οὐσίᾳ· πῶς γὰρ δεῖ νοῆσαι τὸ μὲν ὕστερον τὸ δὲ πρότερον; περὶ μὲν οὖν τῶν κατὰ τὰς διαιρέσεις ὁρισμῶν τοσαῦτα εἰρήσθω τὴν πρώτην, ποῖοί τινές εἰσιν.
notes: "The last differentia is the substance": the definition of man is "two-footed animal" only because "two-footed" already contains "footed" and "animal". The form of the thing is thus one, as the last differentia is one; Book Η (VIII.6) adds that the genus is to the differentia as matter to form.

paragraphs.modern: Since our inquiry is about substance, let us go back to it again. As the underlying thing is said to be substance, and what it is to be, and what is made of these, so too is the universal. About two of these we have spoken: about what it is to be, and about the underlying thing, that it underlies in two ways, either being a this, as the animal underlies its affections, or as the matter underlies the actuality. But the universal too is thought by some to be a cause most of all, and the universal to be a principle; so let us go on to this too. For it seems impossible that any of the things said universally should be substance.
paragraphs.greek: ἐπεὶ δὲ περὶ τῆς οὐσίας ἡ σκέψις ἐστί, πάλιν ἐπανέλθωμεν. λέγεται δʼ ὥσπερ τὸ ὑποκείμενον οὐσία εἶναι καὶ τὸ τί ἦν εἶναι καὶ τὸ ἐκ τούτων, καὶ τὸ καθόλου. περὶ μὲν οὖν τοῖν δυοῖν εἴρηται (καὶ γὰρ περὶ τοῦ τί ἦν εἶναι καὶ τοῦ ὑποκειμένου, ὅτι διχῶς ὑπόκειται, ἢ τόδε τι ὄν, ὥσπερ τὸ ζῷον τοῖς πάθεσιν, ἢ ὡς ἡ ὕλη τῇ ἐντελεχείᾳ), δοκεῖ δὲ καὶ τὸ καθόλου αἴτιόν τισιν εἶναι μάλιστα, καὶ εἶναι ἀρχὴ τὸ καθόλου· διὸ ἐπέλθωμεν καὶ περὶ τούτου. ἔοικε γὰρ ἀδύνατον εἶναι οὐσίαν εἶναι ὁτιοῦν τῶν καθόλου λεγομένων.

flags.taylor: underlies the complete reality
flags.why: Ross's "complete reality" renders ἐντελέχεια, "actuality", the state of having reached its end; Taylor says "energy". The modern version says "actuality", as everywhere in this work.

notes: "Thought by some": the Platonists, for whom the Forms are causes and principles, and are universal (Book Α, I.6 and 9). Chapters 13 to 16 are Aristotle's main argument that the Forms, so taken, are not substances; the Platonists of late antiquity, Syrianus and Proclus, answered that the Forms are not universals in things but causes above them, and that Aristotle's universal is the "later-born" concept in the soul.

paragraphs.modern: First, the substance of each thing is what is peculiar to it, which does not belong to anything else; but the universal is common, for what is called universal is what by nature belongs to more than one. Of which, then, will this be the substance? Either of all, or of none; of all it cannot be; and if of one, the others too will be this one: for things whose substance is one, and whose what-it-is-to-be is one, are themselves one. Again, substance is what is not said of an underlying thing, but the universal is always said of some underlying thing.
paragraphs.greek: πρῶτον μὲν γὰρ οὐσία ἑκάστου ἡ ἴδιος ἑκάστῳ, ἣ οὐχ ὑπάρχει ἄλλῳ, τὸ δὲ καθόλου κοινόν· τοῦτο γὰρ λέγεται καθόλου ὃ πλείοσιν ὑπάρχειν πέφυκεν. τίνος οὖν οὐσία τοῦτʼ ἔσται; ἢ γὰρ πάντων ἢ οὐδενός, πάντων δʼ οὐχ οἷόν τε· ἑνὸς δʼ εἰ ἔσται, καὶ τἆλλα τοῦτʼ ἔσται· ὧν γὰρ μία ἡ οὐσία καὶ τὸ τί ἦν εἶναι ἕν, καὶ αὐτὰ ἕν. ἔτι οὐσία λέγεται τὸ μὴ καθʼ ὑποκειμένου, τὸ δὲ καθόλου καθʼ ὑποκειμένου τινὸς λέγεται ἀεί.

paragraphs.modern: But perhaps the universal cannot be substance in the way what it is to be is, but can be present in it, as animal in man and horse? Then plainly there is some account of it. It makes no difference even if there is not an account of everything in the substance: none the less this will be the substance of something, as man is of the man in whom it is present; so the same will follow again: it will be the substance of that in which it is present as peculiar to it, as animal is. Further, it is impossible and absurd that the this, the substance, if it is made of some things, should be made not of substances, nor of a this, but of a quality: for what is not substance, the quality, will then be prior to substance and to the this. Which is impossible: neither in account, nor in time, nor in coming to be can the affections be prior to the substance; for then they would be separate too. Further, in Socrates there will be a substance present in a substance, so that it will be the substance of two things. And in general it follows, if man and the things said in this way are substance, that nothing in the account is the substance of anything, nor is it apart from them or in anything else: I mean, for instance, that there is no animal besides the particular animals, nor any of the other things in the accounts.
paragraphs.greek: ἀλλʼ ἆρα οὕτω μὲν οὐκ ἐνδέχεται ὡς τὸ τί ἦν εἶναι, ἐν τούτῳ δὲ ἐνυπάρχειν, οἷον τὸ ζῷον ἐν τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ καὶ ἵππῳ; οὐκοῦν δῆλον ὅτι ἔστι τις αὐτοῦ λόγος. διαφέρει δʼ οὐθὲν οὐδʼ εἰ μὴ πάντων λόγος ἔστι τῶν ἐν τῇ οὐσίᾳ· οὐδὲν γὰρ ἧττον οὐσία τοῦτʼ ἔσται τινός, ὡς ὁ ἄνθρωπος τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἐν ᾧ ὑπάρχει, ὥστε τὸ αὐτὸ συμβήσεται πάλιν· ἔσται γὰρ ἐκείνου οὐσία, οἷον τὸ ζῷον, ἐν ᾧ ὡς ἴδιον ὑπάρχει. ἔτι δὲ καὶ ἀδύνατον καὶ ἄτοπον τὸ τόδε καὶ οὐσίαν, εἰ ἔστιν ἔκ τινων, μὴ ἐξ οὐσιῶν εἶναι μηδʼ ἐκ τοῦ τόδε τι ἀλλʼ ἐκ ποιοῦ· πρότερον γὰρ ἔσται μὴ οὐσία τε καὶ τὸ ποιὸν οὐσίας τε καὶ τοῦ τόδε. ὅπερ ἀδύνατον· οὔτε λόγῳ γὰρ οὔτε χρόνῳ οὔτε γενέσει οἷόν τε τὰ πάθη τῆς οὐσίας εἶναι πρότερα· ἔσται γὰρ καὶ χωριστά. ἔτι τῷ Σωκράτει ἐνυπάρξει οὐσία οὐσίᾳ, ὥστε δυοῖν ἔσται οὐσία. ὅλως δὲ συμβαίνει, εἰ ἔστιν οὐσία ὁ ἄνθρωπος καὶ ὅσα οὕτω λέγεται, μηθὲν τῶν ἐν τῷ λόγῳ εἶναι μηδενὸς οὐσίαν μηδὲ χωρὶς ὑπάρχειν αὐτῶν μηδʼ ἐν ἄλλῳ, λέγω δʼ οἷον οὐκ εἶναί τι ζῷον παρὰ τὰ τινά, οὐδʼ ἄλλο τῶν ἐν τοῖς λόγοις οὐδέν.

flags.taylor: nor in time nor in knowledge
flags.why: Ross's 1908 English follows a reading "in knowledge" (γνώσει), as his footnote says; his own Greek of 1924, which the Workshop gives, reads "in coming to be" (γενέσει), as Taylor's Greek did ("generation"). The modern version follows the 1924 text.

flags.taylor: For it is not pofllble that participated properties
flags.why: Taylor's "participated properties" renders πάθη, "affections", the attributes a thing undergoes or has; "participated" is his own word, from the Platonists' language of participation. The modern version says "affections".

paragraphs.modern: Looking at it from these points of view, then, it is plain that nothing that belongs universally is a substance, and that nothing predicated in common signifies a this, but a such. Otherwise many other consequences follow, and among them the third man.
paragraphs.greek: ἔκ τε δὴ τούτων θεωροῦσι φανερὸν ὅτι οὐδὲν τῶν καθόλου ὑπαρχόντων οὐσία ἐστί, καὶ ὅτι οὐδὲν σημαίνει τῶν κοινῇ κατηγορουμένων τόδε τι, ἀλλὰ τοιόνδε. εἰ δὲ μή, ἄλλα τε πολλὰ συμβαίνει καὶ ὁ τρίτος ἄνθρωπος.
notes: The "third man": if man is a this, besides the particular men, then man and the men together call for a further "man" over both, and so without end. Plato's Parmenides (132a-b) raises the same objection against the Forms, with largeness; Aristotle gave it this name in his lost work On the Forms. The Platonists answered that the Form is not one more instance of what it is the Form of.

paragraphs.modern: It is clear in this way too: a substance cannot be made of substances present in it in actuality. For two things that are actually two are never actually one; but if they are potentially two, they will be one (as the double line is made of two halves, potentially at least: for actuality separates). So if the substance is one, it will not be made of substances present in it, and in this way; as Democritus rightly says, it is impossible for one to come to be from two, or two from one; for he makes the indivisible magnitudes the substances. It is plain, then, that it will be likewise with number, if number is a putting together of units, as some say: either the dyad is not one, or there is no unit in it in actuality.
paragraphs.greek: ἔτι δὲ καὶ ὧδε δῆλον. ἀδύνατον γὰρ οὐσίαν ἐξ οὐσιῶν εἶναι ἐνυπαρχουσῶν ὡς ἐντελεχείᾳ· τὰ γὰρ δύο οὕτως ἐντελεχείᾳ οὐδέποτε ἓν ἐντελεχείᾳ, ἀλλʼ ἐὰν δυνάμει δύο ᾖ, ἔσται ἕν (οἷον ἡ διπλασία ἐκ δύο ἡμίσεων δυνάμει γε· ἡ γὰρ ἐντελέχεια χωρίζει), ὥστʼ εἰ ἡ οὐσία ἕν, οὐκ ἔσται ἐξ οὐσιῶν ἐνυπαρχουσῶν καὶ κατὰ τοῦτον τὸν τρόπον, ὃν λέγει Δημόκριτος ὀρθῶς· ἀδύνατον γὰρ εἶναί φησιν ἐκ δύο ἓν ἢ ἐξ ἑνὸς δύο γενέσθαι· τὰ γὰρ μεγέθη τὰ ἄτομα τὰς οὐσίας ποιεῖ. ὁμοίως τοίνυν δῆλον ὅτι καὶ ἐπʼ ἀριθμοῦ ἕξει, εἴπερ ἐστὶν ὁ ἀριθμὸς σύνθεσις μονάδων, ὥσπερ λέγεται ὑπό τινων· ἢ γὰρ οὐχ ἓν ἡ δυὰς ἢ οὐκ ἔστι μονὰς ἐν αὐτῇ ἐντελεχείᾳ.—
notes: Democritus' atoms are substances, and so, he said, two atoms never become one. Aristotle agrees with the principle and draws the opposite moral: a substance that is one must not contain substances actually, but only potentially, as a line contains its halves until it is cut.

paragraphs.modern: What follows involves a puzzle. If no substance can be made of universals, because they signify a such and not a this, and no substance can be composed of substances in actuality, every substance would be incomposite, so that there would be no account of any substance. But it is thought by all, and was said long ago, that there is a definition either of substance only, or of it most of all; and now not even of this. So there will be a definition of nothing. Or rather, in one way there will be, and in another not. What is meant will be clearer from what follows.
paragraphs.greek: ἔχει δὲ τὸ συμβαῖνον ἀπορίαν. εἰ γὰρ μήτε ἐκ τῶν καθόλου οἷόν τʼ εἶναι μηδεμίαν οὐσίαν διὰ τὸ τοιόνδε ἀλλὰ μὴ τόδε τι σημαίνειν, μήτʼ ἐξ οὐσιῶν ἐνδέχεται ἐντελεχείᾳ εἶναι μηδεμίαν οὐσίαν σύνθετον, ἀσύνθετον ἂν εἴη οὐσία πᾶσα, ὥστʼ οὐδὲ λόγος ἂν εἴη οὐδεμιᾶς οὐσίας. ἀλλὰ μὴν δοκεῖ γε πᾶσι καὶ ἐλέχθη πάλαι ἢ μόνον οὐσίας εἶναι ὅρον ἢ μάλιστα· νῦν δʼ οὐδὲ ταύτης. οὐδενὸς ἄρʼ ἔσται ὁρισμός· ἢ τρόπον μέν τινα ἔσται τρόπον δέ τινα οὔ. δῆλον δʼ ἔσται τὸ λεγόμενον ἐκ τῶν ὕστερον μᾶλλον.
notes: "From what follows": chapters 15 and 17 of this book, and Book Η (VIII.6), where the definition is one because the genus is as matter, potential, and the differentia as form, actual.

paragraphs.modern: From these same considerations it is plain what follows for those who say the Forms are substances and separate, and at the same time make the Form out of the genus and the differentiae. For if there are Forms, and "animal" is in "man" and "horse", it is either one and the same in number with itself, or different. In account it is plainly one: whoever states it goes through the same account in either case. If, then, there is a man himself by himself, a this and separate, the things he is made of, such as "animal" and "two-footed", must also signify a this and be separate and substances: so "animal" too.
paragraphs.greek: φανερὸν δʼ ἐξ αὐτῶν τούτων τὸ συμβαῖνον καὶ τοῖς τὰς ἰδέας λέγουσιν οὐσίας τε χωριστὰς εἶναι καὶ ἅμα τὸ εἶδος ἐκ τοῦ γένους ποιοῦσι καὶ τῶν διαφορῶν. εἰ γὰρ ἔστι τὰ εἴδη, καὶ τὸ ζῷον ἐν τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ καὶ ἵππῳ, ἤτοι ἓν καὶ ταὐτὸν τῷ ἀριθμῷ ἐστὶν ἢ ἕτερον· τῷ μὲν γὰρ λόγῳ δῆλον ὅτι ἕν· τὸν γὰρ αὐτὸν διέξεισι λόγον ὁ λέγων ἐν ἑκατέρῳ. εἰ οὖν ἐστί τις ἄνθρωπος αὐτὸς καθʼ αὑτὸν τόδε τι καὶ κεχωρισμένον, ἀνάγκη καὶ ἐξ ὧν, οἷον τὸ ζῷον καὶ τὸ δίπουν, τόδε τι σημαίνειν καὶ εἶναι χωριστὰ καὶ οὐσίας· ὥστε καὶ τὸ ζῷον.
notes: "Man himself" (αὐτὸς ὁ ἄνθρωπος): the Form of man, in the Academy's way of naming the Forms, "itself by itself" (Phaedo 78d, Symposium 211b).

paragraphs.modern: If, then, the animal in the horse and in the man is one and the same, as you are with yourself, how will what is one in things that are apart be one, and why will this animal not also be apart from itself? Then, if it is to share in the two-footed and the many-footed, something impossible follows: contraries will belong at once to it, though it is one and a this. And if it does not, what is the way in which one says the animal is two-footed or footed? Perhaps they are put together and touch, or are mixed? But all these are absurd.
paragraphs.greek: εἰ μὲν οὖν τὸ αὐτὸ καὶ ἓν τὸ ἐν τῷ ἵππῳ καὶ τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ, ὥσπερ σὺ σαυτῷ, πῶς τὸ ἓν ἐν τοῖς οὖσι χωρὶς ἓν ἔσται, καὶ διὰ τί οὐ καὶ χωρὶς αὑτοῦ ἔσται τὸ ζῷον τοῦτο; ἔπειτα εἰ μὲν μεθέξει τοῦ δίποδος καὶ τοῦ πολύποδος, ἀδύνατόν τι συμβαίνει, τἀναντία γὰρ ἅμα ὑπάρξει αὐτῷ ἑνὶ καὶ τῷδέ τινι ὄντι· εἰ δὲ μή, τίς ὁ τρόπος ὅταν εἴπῃ τις τὸ ζῷον εἶναι δίπουν ἢ πεζόν; ἀλλʼ ἴσως σύγκειται καὶ ἅπτεται ἢ μέμικται· ἀλλὰ πάντα ἄτοπα.

flags.taylor: if it participates of biped and multiped
flags.why: Taylor's words are right: μεθέξει is "will share in", "will participate in", the Platonists' word for the relation of things to Forms, here turned against a Form that would have to share in contrary Forms. The modern version says "share in".

paragraphs.modern: But suppose it is different in each. Then there will be, one might say, unlimited things whose substance is animal: for man is not made of animal by accident. Further, animal itself will be many. For the animal in each is substance (it is not said by virtue of something else; otherwise man would be made of that, and that would be his genus); and further, all the things man is made of will be Forms. So it will not be the Form of one thing and the substance of another (that is impossible): each of those in the animals, then, will be animal itself. Further, from what will this be made, and how from animal itself? Or how can that animal, whose substance is just this, be besides animal itself? Further, in the case of sensible things these consequences follow, and others more absurd still. If, then, it is impossible for things to be so, it is plain that there are not Forms of them in the way some say.
paragraphs.greek: ἀλλʼ ἕτερον ἐν ἑκάστῳ· οὐκοῦν ἄπειρα ὡς ἔπος εἰπεῖν ἔσται ὧν ἡ οὐσία ζῷον· οὐ γὰρ κατὰ συμβεβηκὸς ἐκ ζῴου ἅνθρωπος. ἔτι πολλὰ ἔσται αὐτὸ τὸ ζῷον· οὐσία τε γὰρ τὸ ἐν ἑκάστῳ ζῷον (οὐ γὰρ κατʼ ἄλλο λέγεται· εἰ δὲ μή, ἐξ ἐκείνου ἔσται ὁ ἄνθρωπος καὶ γένος αὐτοῦ ἐκεῖνο), καὶ ἔτι ἰδέαι ἅπαντα ἐξ ὧν ὁ ἄνθρωπος· οὐκοῦν οὐκ ἄλλου μὲν ἰδέα ἔσται ἄλλου δʼ οὐσία (ἀδύνατον γάρ)· αὐτὸ ἄρα ζῷον ἓν ἕκαστον ἔσται τῶν ἐν τοῖς ζῴοις. ἔτι ἐκ τίνος τοῦτο, καὶ πῶς ἐξ αὐτοῦ ζῴου; ἢ πῶς οἷόν τε εἶναι τὸ ζῷον, ᾧ οὐσία τοῦτο αὐτό, παρʼ αὐτὸ τὸ ζῷον; ἔτι δʼ ἐπὶ τῶν αἰσθητῶν ταῦτά τε συμβαίνει καὶ τούτων ἀτοπώτερα. εἰ δὴ ἀδύνατον οὕτως ἔχειν, δῆλον ὅτι οὐκ ἔστιν εἴδη αὐτῶν οὕτως ὥς τινές φασιν.

flags.taylor: Each, then, of the Ideas present in the species of animals will be the ideal animal
flags.why: Ross's "the ideal animal" renders αὐτὸ ζῷον, "animal itself", the Academy's name for the Form of animal; Plato's Timaeus (30c-31b, 39e) calls the model of the cosmos "the living thing itself" (αὐτὸ ὃ ἔστι ζῷον), which the Platonists set at the summit of the intelligible world. The modern version says "animal itself".

notes: The dilemma: the Form "animal" in "man" and "horse" is either one (and then one thing is in many separate things, and has contrary attributes) or many (and then there are unlimited "animals themselves"). Plato's Parmenides (131a-c) puts the first horn to Socrates with the day and the sail; Proclus' commentary answers that the Forms are present to things without being divided, as the day is.

paragraphs.modern: Since substance is of two kinds, the compound and the account (I mean that one is substance as the account taken together with the matter, the other as the account in general), the substances said in the first way can perish (for they can also come to be); but the account is not such as to perish (for it does not come to be either: being a house does not come to be, but being this house); they are and are not without coming to be and perishing, for it has been shown that no one begets or makes them. That is why there is neither definition nor demonstration of particular perceptible substances: they have matter, whose nature is such that it can both be and not be; so all the particular ones among them perish. If, then, demonstration is of what is necessary, and definition belongs to knowledge, and just as knowledge cannot be sometimes knowledge and sometimes ignorance, but what is such is opinion, so there can be neither demonstration nor definition of these, but opinion is of what can be otherwise, clearly there can be neither definition nor demonstration of them. For perishable things are unclear to those who have knowledge of them, when they pass out of perception; and though the accounts are kept in the soul, there will no longer be either definition or demonstration of them. So when someone who deals with definitions defines some particular, he must not forget that it can always be undone: for it is not possible to define it.
paragraphs.greek: ἐπεὶ δʼ ἡ οὐσία ἑτέρα, τό τε σύνολον καὶ ὁ λόγος (λέγω δʼ ὅτι ἡ μὲν οὕτως ἐστὶν οὐσία, σὺν τῇ ὕλῃ συνειλημμένος ὁ λόγος, ἡ δʼ ὁ λόγος ὅλως), ὅσαι μὲν οὖν οὕτω λέγονται, τούτων μὲν ἔστι φθορά (καὶ γὰρ γένεσις), τοῦ δὲ λόγου οὐκ ἔστιν οὕτως ὥστε φθείρεσθαι (οὐδὲ γὰρ γένεσις, οὐ γὰρ γίγνεται τὸ οἰκίᾳ εἶναι ἀλλὰ τὸ τῇδε τῇ οἰκίᾳ), ἀλλʼ ἄνευ γενέσεως καὶ φθορᾶς εἰσὶ καὶ οὐκ εἰσίν· δέδεικται γὰρ ὅτι οὐδεὶς ταῦτα γεννᾷ οὐδὲ ποιεῖ. διὰ τοῦτο δὲ καὶ τῶν οὐσιῶν τῶν αἰσθητῶν τῶν καθʼ ἕκαστα οὔτε ὁρισμὸς οὔτε ἀπόδειξις ἔστιν, ὅτι ἔχουσιν ὕλην ἧς ἡ φύσις τοιαύτη ὥστʼ ἐνδέχεσθαι καὶ εἶναι καὶ μή· διὸ φθαρτὰ πάντα τὰ καθʼ ἕκαστα αὐτῶν. εἰ οὖν ἥ τʼ ἀπόδειξις τῶν ἀναγκαίων καὶ ὁ ὁρισμὸς ἐπιστημονικόν, καὶ οὐκ ἐνδέχεται, ὥσπερ οὐδʼ ἐπιστήμην ὁτὲ μὲν ἐπιστήμην ὁτὲ δʼ ἄγνοιαν εἶναι, ἀλλὰ δόξα τὸ τοιοῦτόν ἐστιν, οὕτως οὐδʼ ἀπόδειξιν οὐδʼ ὁρισμόν, ἀλλὰ δόξα ἐστὶ τοῦ ἐνδεχομένου ἄλλως ἔχειν, δῆλον ὅτι οὐκ ἂν εἴη αὐτῶν οὔτε ὁρισμὸς οὔτε ἀπόδειξις. ἄδηλά τε γὰρ τὰ φθειρόμενα τοῖς ἔχουσι τὴν ἐπιστήμην, ὅταν ἐκ τῆς αἰσθήσεως ἀπέλθῃ, καὶ σωζομένων τῶν λόγων ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ τῶν αὐτῶν οὐκ ἔσται οὔτε ὁρισμὸς ἔτι οὔτε ἀπόδειξις. διὸ δεῖ, τῶν πρὸς ὅρον ὅταν τις ὁρίζηταί τι τῶν καθʼ ἕκαστον, μὴ ἀγνοεῖν ὅτι ἀεὶ ἀναιρεῖν ἔστιν· οὐ γὰρ ἐνδέχεται ὁρίσασθαι.
notes: Knowledge (ἐπιστήμη) is of what cannot be otherwise; opinion (δόξα) of what can. The line is Plato's (Republic V, 476d-480a; Timaeus 27d-28a): what always is is grasped by intellect with an account, what comes to be and perishes by opinion with perception. Aristotle keeps the line and draws it within the sensible thing, between its form and its matter.

paragraphs.modern: Nor, then, can any Form be defined. For the Form is, as they say, a particular, and separate; and the account must be made of names, but the one defining will not make a name (for it will be unknown), and the names laid down are common to all things; so these must belong to something else too. If one were to define you, for instance, he would say "an animal, lean" or "pale", or something else that will belong to another too. If someone should say that nothing prevents all of them belonging, taken apart, to many things, but together to this alone, we must say first that they belong to both of the elements too: "two-footed animal" belongs to animal and to the two-footed. (In eternal things this must even be so, since the elements are prior and parts of the compound; and indeed they are separate too, if "man" is separate: either neither is, or both are. If neither, the genus will not be besides the species; if it is, the differentia will be too.) Next, they are prior in being; and these are not taken away with the compound.
paragraphs.greek: οὐδὲ δὴ ἰδέαν οὐδεμίαν ἔστιν ὁρίσασθαι. τῶν γὰρ καθʼ ἕκαστον ἡ ἰδέα, ὡς φασί, καὶ χωριστή· ἀναγκαῖον δὲ ἐξ ὀνομάτων εἶναι τὸν λόγον, ὄνομα δʼ οὐ ποιήσει ὁ ὁριζόμενος (ἄγνωστον γὰρ ἔσται), τὰ δὲ κείμενα κοινὰ πᾶσιν· ἀνάγκη ἄρα ὑπάρχειν καὶ ἄλλῳ ταῦτα· οἷον εἴ τις σὲ ὁρίσαιτο, ζῷον ἐρεῖ ἰσχνὸν ἢ λευκὸν ἢ ἕτερόν τι ὃ καὶ ἄλλῳ ὑπάρξει. εἰ δέ τις φαίη μηδὲν κωλύειν χωρὶς μὲν πάντα πολλοῖς ἅμα δὲ μόνῳ τούτῳ ὑπάρχειν, λεκτέον πρῶτον μὲν ὅτι καὶ ἀμφοῖν, οἷον τὸ ζῷον δίπουν τῷ ζῴῳ καὶ τῷ δίποδι (καὶ τοῦτο ἐπὶ μὲν τῶν ἀϊδίων καὶ ἀνάγκη εἶναι, πρότερά γʼ ὄντα καὶ μέρη τοῦ συνθέτου· ἀλλὰ μὴν καὶ χωριστά, εἴπερ τὸ ἄνθρωπος χωριστόν· ἢ γὰρ οὐθὲν ἢ ἄμφω· εἰ μὲν οὖν μηθέν, οὐκ ἔσται τὸ γένος παρὰ τὰ εἴδη, εἰ δʼ ἔσται, καὶ ἡ διαφορά)· εἶθʼ ὅτι πρότερα τῷ εἶναι· ταῦτα δὲ οὐκ ἀνταναιρεῖται.
notes: The argument turns on the Platonists' own account: if the Form of man is "two-footed animal", its parts, the Form of animal and the Form of two-footed, belong to other things too, and are prior; so the definition fits more than the one Form, and the Form, as a particular, has no definition proper to it.

paragraphs.modern: Then, if the Forms are made of Forms (for the things they are made of are less composite), the things the Form is made of, as animal and two-footed, will also have to be predicated of many. If not, how will they be known? For there will be a Form that cannot be predicated of more than one. But that is not thought to be so: every Form is thought to be shareable. As has been said, then, it escapes notice that it is impossible to define in the case of eternal things, above all those that are unique, such as the sun or the moon. People go wrong not only by adding things which can be taken away and the sun still be, as "going round the earth" or "hidden at night" (for if it stood still or shone at night, it would no longer be the sun; but it is absurd if not, since "the sun" signifies a certain substance); but also by adding what can belong to something else: if another thing of the kind came to be, plainly it would be a sun. So the account is common. But the sun was one of the particulars, like Cleon or Socrates. Why does none of those who posit the Forms bring out a definition of one of them? If they tried, it would become clear that what has now been said is true.
paragraphs.greek: ἔπειτα εἰ ἐξ ἰδεῶν αἱ ἰδέαι (ἁσυνθετώτερα γὰρ τὰ ἐξ ὧν), ἔτι ἐπὶ πολλῶν δεήσει κἀκεῖνα κατηγορεῖσθαι ἐξ ὧν ἡ ἰδέα, οἷον τὸ ζῷον καὶ τὸ δίπουν. εἰ δὲ μή, πῶς γνωρισθήσεται; ἔσται γὰρ ἰδέα τις ἣν ἀδύνατον ἐπὶ πλειόνων κατηγορῆσαι ἢ ἑνός. οὐ δοκεῖ δέ, ἀλλὰ πᾶσα ἰδέα εἶναι μεθεκτή. ὥσπερ οὖν εἴρηται, λανθάνει ὅτι ἀδύνατον ὁρίσασθαι ἐν τοῖς ἀϊδίοις, μάλιστα δὲ ὅσα μοναχά, οἷον ἥλιος ἢ σελήνη. οὐ μόνον γὰρ διαμαρτάνουσι τῷ προστιθέναι τοιαῦτα ὧν ἀφαιρουμένων ἔτι ἔσται ἥλιος, ὥσπερ τὸ περὶ γῆν ἰὸν ἢ νυκτικρυφές (ἂν γὰρ στῇ ἢ φανῇ, οὐκέτι ἔσται ἥλιος· ἀλλʼ ἄτοπον εἰ μή· ὁ γὰρ ἥλιος οὐσίαν τινὰ σημαίνεi)· ἔτι ὅσα ἐπʼ ἄλλου ἐνδέχεται, οἷον ἐὰν ἕτερος γένηται τοιοῦτος, δῆλον ὅτι ἥλιος ἔσται· κοινὸς ἄρα ὁ λόγος· ἀλλʼ ἦν τῶν καθʼ ἕκαστα ὁ ἥλιος, ὥσπερ Κλέων ἢ Σωκράτης· ἐπεὶ διὰ τί οὐδεὶς ὅρον ἐκφέρει αὐτῶν ἰδέας; γένοιτο γὰρ ἂν δῆλον πειρωμένων ὅτι ἀληθὲς τὸ νῦν εἰρημένον.

flags.taylor: to be capable of being shared
flags.why: Ross's words are right: μεθεκτή, "shareable", "participable", is the Platonists' own word, and it makes the Form a universal, said of many, against its being a particular. Proclus (Elements of Theology, props. 23-24) distinguished the unparticipated Form from the participated, to meet arguments of this kind.

notes: Cleon, the Athenian leader of the Peloponnesian war, here a stock example of a particular man, as Socrates is.

paragraphs.modern: It is plain that even of the things thought to be substances, most are potencies: the parts of animals (none of them is separated; and when they are separated, then too they all are as matter), and earth, fire and air; for none of them is one, but they are like a heap, until they are concocted and something one comes to be out of them. One might suppose above all that the parts of living things, and the parts of the soul close to them, are both, being in actuality and in potency, because they have principles of motion from something in their joints; which is why some animals live when they are cut in two. Yet they will all be in potency, when they are one and continuous by nature, not by force or by growing together; for such a thing is a deformity.
paragraphs.greek: φανερὸν δὲ ὅτι καὶ τῶν δοκουσῶν εἶναι οὐσιῶν αἱ πλεῖσται δυνάμεις εἰσί, τά τε μόρια τῶν ζῴων (οὐθὲν γὰρ κεχωρισμένον αὐτῶν ἐστίν· ὅταν δὲ χωρισθῇ, καὶ τότε ὄντα ὡς ὕλη πάντα) καὶ γῆ καὶ πῦρ καὶ ἀήρ· οὐδὲν γὰρ αὐτῶν ἕν ἐστιν, ἀλλʼ οἷον σωρός, πρὶν ἢ πεφθῇ καὶ γένηταί τι ἐξ αὐτῶν ἕν. μάλιστα δʼ ἄν τις τὰ τῶν ἐμψύχων ὑπολάβοι μόρια καὶ τὰ τῆς ψυχῆς πάρεγγυς ἄμφω γίγνεσθαι, ὄντα καὶ ἐντελεχείᾳ καὶ δυνάμει, τῷ ἀρχὰς ἔχειν κινήσεως ἀπό τινος ἐν ταῖς καμπαῖς· διὸ ἔνια ζῷα διαιρούμενα ζῇ. ἀλλʼ ὅμως δυνάμει πάντʼ ἔσται, ὅταν ᾖ ἓν καὶ συνεχὲς φύσει, ἀλλὰ μὴ βίᾳ ἢ συμφύσει· τὸ γὰρ τοιοῦτον πήρωσις.

flags.taylor: are only so in capacity
flags.why: Taylor's "capacity" renders δυνάμει, "in potency", against "in actuality"; the parts of a living thing, while it lives, are not things of their own but potentially so. The modern version says "potency", as everywhere in this work.

notes: "Some animals live when cut in two": insects and worms, which On Youth and Old Age (468a-b) and On the Soul (I.5, 411b19-27) take as signs that the soul is present whole in each part. Plotinus (IV.2.1) uses the same fact for the soul's being undivided in the divided body.

paragraphs.modern: Since "one" is said as "being" is, and the substance of what is one is one, and things whose substance is one in number are one in number, it is plain that neither the one nor being can be the substance of things, just as being an element or a principle cannot; but we seek what, then, the principle is, so that we may bring the matter back to something better known. Of these, being and one are more substance than principle, element and cause; but not even these are, if nothing else common is substance either: for substance belongs to nothing but itself and to what has it, whose substance it is. Further, what is one cannot be in many places at once, but what is common belongs to many at once; so that it is clear that no universal is separately, besides the particulars.
paragraphs.greek: ἐπεὶ δὲ τὸ ἓν λέγεται ὥσπερ καὶ τὸ ὄν, καὶ ἡ οὐσία ἡ τοῦ ἑνὸς μία, καὶ ὧν μία ἀριθμῷ ἓν ἀριθμῷ, φανερὸν ὅτι οὔτε τὸ ἓν οὔτε τὸ ὂν ἐνδέχεται οὐσίαν εἶναι τῶν πραγμάτων, ὥσπερ οὐδὲ τὸ στοιχείῳ εἶναι ἢ ἀρχῇ· ἀλλὰ ζητοῦμεν τίς οὖν ἡ ἀρχή, ἵνα εἰς γνωριμώτερον ἀναγάγωμεν. μᾶλλον μὲν οὖν τούτων οὐσία τὸ ὂν καὶ ἓν ἢ ἥ τε ἀρχὴ καὶ τὸ στοιχεῖον καὶ τὸ αἴτιον, οὔπω δὲ οὐδὲ ταῦτα, εἴπερ μηδʼ ἄλλο κοινὸν μηδὲν οὐσία· οὐδενὶ γὰρ ὑπάρχει ἡ οὐσία ἀλλʼ ἢ αὑτῇ τε καὶ τῷ ἔχοντι αὐτήν, οὗ ἐστὶν οὐσία. ἔτι τὸ ἓν πολλαχῇ οὐκ ἂν εἴη ἅμα, τὸ δὲ κοινὸν ἅμα πολλαχῇ ὑπάρχει· ὥστε δῆλον ὅτι οὐδὲν τῶν καθόλου ὑπάρχει παρὰ τὰ καθʼ ἕκαστα χωρίς.
notes: Against the Platonists and the Pythagoreans who made the One and Being the substance of things (Book Β, III.4, the eleventh puzzle; Book Ι, X.2, answers it). For the Platonists of late antiquity the One is not a substance at all but beyond substance (Republic 509b), and so the argument did not touch their first principle; Syrianus says as much in his commentary on these books.

paragraphs.modern: But those who speak of the Forms are right in one way, in separating them, if they are substances; and wrong in another, because they say the one over many is a Form. The reason is that they cannot say what such substances are, the imperishable ones besides the particular and perceptible ones. So they make them the same in form as the perishable ones (for these we know), "man himself" and "horse himself", adding to the perceptible things the word "itself". And yet, even if we had not seen the stars, there would none the less, I suppose, have been eternal substances besides those we knew; so now too, even if we cannot say what they are, it is perhaps necessary that there be some. It is clear, then, that none of the things said universally is substance, and that no substance is made of substances.
paragraphs.greek: ἀλλʼ οἱ τὰ εἴδη λέγοντες τῇ μὲν ὀρθῶς λέγουσι χωρίζοντες αὐτά, εἴπερ οὐσίαι εἰσί, τῇ δʼ οὐκ ὀρθῶς, ὅτι τὸ ἓν ἐπὶ πολλῶν εἶδος λέγουσιν. αἴτιον δʼ ὅτι οὐκ ἔχουσιν ἀποδοῦναι τίνες αἱ τοιαῦται οὐσίαι αἱ ἄφθαρτοι παρὰ τὰς καθʼ ἕκαστα καὶ αἰσθητάς· ποιοῦσιν οὖν τὰς αὐτὰς τῷ εἴδει τοῖς φθαρτοῖς (ταύτας γὰρ ἴσμεν), αὐτοάνθρωπον καὶ αὐτόϊππον, προστιθέντες τοῖς αἰσθητοῖς τὸ ῥῆμα τὸ αὐτό. καίτοι κἂν εἰ μὴ ἑωράκειμεν τὰ ἄστρα, οὐδὲν ἂν ἧττον, οἶμαι, ἦσαν οὐσίαι ἀΐδιοι παρʼ ἃς ἡμεῖς ᾔδειμεν· ὥστε καὶ νῦν εἰ μὴ ἔχομεν τίνες εἰσίν, ἀλλʼ εἶναί γέ τινας ἴσως ἀναγκαῖον. ὅτι μὲν οὖν οὔτε τῶν καθόλου λεγομένων οὐδὲν οὐσία οὔτʼ ἐστὶν οὐσία οὐδεμία ἐξ οὐσιῶν, δῆλον.
notes: "Right to separate them": Aristotle grants the Platonists that there are eternal, separate substances; he denies that they are universals, copies of perishable things with "itself" added. Book Λ (XII.6-10) gives his own account of them: the unmoved movers, intellects in actuality. The Platonists read the line as Aristotle's agreement with them on the main point.

paragraphs.modern: What, and of what kind, substance should be said to be, let us state again, making another start, as it were: for perhaps from this it will be clear too about that substance which is separate from the perceptible substances. Since, then, substance is a principle and a cause, let us proceed from there. The "why" is always sought in this way: why does one thing belong to another? To seek why the musical man is a musical man is either to seek, as has been said, why the man is musical, or something else. To seek why a thing is itself is to seek nothing (for the fact, that it is, must already be clear, as that the moon is eclipsed; and that a thing is itself is the one account and the one cause for all such questions, why the man is a man or the musical musical, unless one were to say that each thing is undivided from itself, and this was what being one is; but that is common to all and a short way). But one might ask why a man is an animal of such a kind. Here, then, it is clear that one is not asking why he who is a man is a man. One is asking, then, why something belongs to something (that it belongs must be clear; if not, one is asking nothing): for instance, why does it thunder? Why does a noise come about in the clouds? For in this way what is sought is one thing said of another. And why are these things, bricks and stones, a house?
paragraphs.greek: τί δὲ χρὴ λέγειν καὶ ὁποῖόν τι τὴν οὐσίαν, πάλιν ἄλλην οἷον ἀρχὴν ποιησάμενοι λέγωμεν· ἴσως γὰρ ἐκ τούτων ἔσται δῆλον καὶ περὶ ἐκείνης τῆς οὐσίας ἥτις ἐστὶ κεχωρισμένη τῶν αἰσθητῶν οὐσιῶν. ἐπεὶ οὖν ἡ οὐσία ἀρχὴ καὶ αἰτία τις ἐστίν, ἐντεῦθεν μετιτέον. ζητεῖται δὲ τὸ διὰ τί ἀεὶ οὕτως, διὰ τί ἄλλο ἄλλῳ τινὶ ὑπάρχει. τὸ γὰρ ζητεῖν διὰ τί ὁ μουσικὸς ἄνθρωπος μουσικὸς ἄνθρωπός ἐστιν, ἤτοι ἐστὶ τὸ εἰρημένον ζητεῖν, διὰ τί ὁ ἄνθρωπος μουσικός ἐστιν, ἢ ἄλλο. τὸ μὲν οὖν διὰ τί αὐτό ἐστιν αὐτό, οὐδέν ἐστι ζητεῖν (δεῖ γὰρ τὸ ὅτι καὶ τὸ εἶναι ὑπάρχειν δῆλα ὄντα—λέγω δʼ οἷον ὅτι ἡ σελήνη ἐκλείπει—, αὐτὸ δὲ ὅτι αὐτό, εἷς λόγος καὶ μία αἰτία ἐπὶ πάντων, διὰ τί ὁ ἄνθρωπος ἄνθρωπος ἢ ὁ μουσικὸς μουσικός, πλὴν εἴ τις λέγοι ὅτι ἀδιαίρετον πρὸς αὑτὸ ἕκαστον, τοῦτο δʼ ἦν τὸ ἑνὶ εἶναι· ἀλλὰ τοῦτο κοινόν γε κατὰ πάντων καὶ σύντομον)· ζητήσειε δʼ ἄν τις διὰ τί ἅνθρωπός ἐστι ζῷον τοιονδί. τοῦτο μὲν τοίνυν δῆλον, ὅτι οὐ ζητεῖ διὰ τί ὅς ἐστιν ἄνθρωπος ἄνθρωπός ἐστιν· τὶ ἄρα κατά τινος ζητεῖ διὰ τί ὑπάρχει (ὅτι δʼ ὑπάρχει, δεῖ δῆλον εἶναι· εἰ γὰρ μὴ οὕτως, οὐδὲν ζητεῖ), οἷον διὰ τί βροντᾷ; διὰ τί ψόφος γίγνεται ἐν τοῖς νέφεσιν; ἄλλο γὰρ οὕτω κατʼ ἄλλου ἐστὶ τὸ ζητούμενον. καὶ διὰ τί ταδί, οἷον πλίνθοι καὶ λίθοι, οἰκία ἐστίν;

flags.taylor: Let us state what should be said to be the genus and the differentia of substance
flags.why: The Greek asks "what, and of what kind" (τί καὶ ὁποῖόν τι) substance should be said to be; Ross's English makes the two words the genus and the differentia of substance, which is his gloss. Taylor says "what, and what kind of a thing".

notes: "Why is the moon eclipsed?" is the model question of the Posterior Analytics (II.2, 90a15-18; II.8): the answer, the earth's coming between, is the middle term, the cause, and also what the eclipse is. This chapter carries that model over to substance.

paragraphs.modern: It is plain, then, that one is seeking the cause. And this is what it is to be, to speak in the manner of argument about words: in some things it is that for the sake of which, as perhaps in a house or a bed, and in some the first thing that moved; for this too is a cause. But this second kind of cause is sought in coming to be and perishing, the other in being too. What is sought escapes notice most in things not said one of another, as when one asks what a man is, because it is said simply and one does not mark off that these things are this. But one must articulate the question before seeking; otherwise it becomes something between seeking nothing and seeking something. Since the being must be had and must belong, it is clear that one is asking about the matter, why it is something: why are these things a house? Because what it is to be a house belongs to them. And why is this, or this body having this, a man? So what is sought is the cause of the matter (and this is the form) by which it is something; and this is the substance. It is plain, then, that in the case of simple things there is no seeking nor teaching, but another way of inquiring into such things.
paragraphs.greek: φανερὸν τοίνυν ὅτι ζητεῖ τὸ αἴτιον· τοῦτο δʼ ἐστὶ τὸ τί ἦν εἶναι, ὡς εἰπεῖν λογικῶς, ὃ ἐπʼ ἐνίων μέν ἐστι τίνος ἕνεκα, οἷον ἴσως ἐπʼ οἰκίας ἢ κλίνης, ἐπʼ ἐνίων δὲ τί ἐκίνησε πρῶτον· αἴτιον γὰρ καὶ τοῦτο. ἀλλὰ τὸ μὲν τοιοῦτον αἴτιον ἐπὶ τοῦ γίγνεσθαι ζητεῖται καὶ φθείρεσθαι, θάτερον δὲ καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ εἶναι. λανθάνει δὲ μάλιστα τὸ ζητούμενον ἐν τοῖς μὴ κατʼ ἀλλήλων λεγομένοις, οἷον ἄνθρωπος τί ἐστι ζητεῖται διὰ τὸ ἁπλῶς λέγεσθαι ἀλλὰ μὴ διορίζειν ὅτι τάδε τόδε. ἀλλὰ δεῖ διαρθρώσαντας ζητεῖν· εἰ δὲ μή, κοινὸν τοῦ μηθὲν ζητεῖν καὶ τοῦ ζητεῖν τι γίγνεται. ἐπεὶ δὲ δεῖ ἔχειν τε καὶ ὑπάρχειν τὸ εἶναι, δῆλον δὴ ὅτι τὴν ὕλην ζητεῖ διὰ τί τί ἐστιν· οἷον οἰκία ταδὶ διὰ τί; ὅτι ὑπάρχει ὃ ἦν οἰκίᾳ εἶναι. καὶ ἄνθρωπος τοδί, ἢ τὸ σῶμα τοῦτο τοδὶ ἔχον. ὥστε τὸ αἴτιον ζητεῖται τῆς ὕλης (τοῦτο δʼ ἐστὶ τὸ εἶδος) ᾧ τί ἐστιν· τοῦτο δʼ ἡ οὐσία. φανερὸν τοίνυν ὅτι ἐπὶ τῶν ἁπλῶν οὐκ ἔστι ζήτησις οὐδὲ δίδαξις, ἀλλʼ ἕτερος τρόπος τῆς ζητήσεως τῶν τοιούτων.—

flags.taylor: But while the efficient cause is sought in the case of genesis and destruction
flags.why: Ross names the two causes with the later schools' words, "efficient" and "final"; the Greek says only "such a cause" (the first mover) and "the other" (that for the sake of which, which is the form). The modern version keeps the Greek's plainer words.

notes: "Simple things": things not composed of matter and form, which have no cause other than themselves; they are known not by seeking a middle term but by direct grasp, as Book Θ (IX.10) says of the truth of simple things, "touching" and "saying".

paragraphs.modern: Since what is composed of something in such a way that the whole is one, not like a heap but like a syllable (and the syllable is not its letters, nor is "ba" the same as b and a, nor is flesh fire and earth: for when they are broken up, the wholes, the flesh and the syllable, no longer are, but the letters are, and fire and earth), the syllable, then, is something, not only its letters, the vowel and the consonant, but something else too; and flesh is not only fire and earth, or the hot and the cold, but something else too. If, then, that something must be either an element or made of elements: if an element, the same argument will apply again (flesh will be made of this and fire and earth and something else, so that it will go on without end); and if made of elements, plainly not of one but of more (or else it will be that one itself), so that again we will say the same about it as about the flesh or the syllable. But it would seem that this is something, and not an element, and is the cause of this being flesh and that a syllable; and likewise in the other cases. And this is the substance of each thing: for this is the first cause of its being. And since some things are not substances, but those that are substances are formed according to nature and by nature, this nature too would appear to be substance, which is not an element but a principle. An element is what a thing is divided into, present in it as matter, as a and b of the syllable.
paragraphs.greek: ἐπεὶ δὲ τὸ ἔκ τινος σύνθετον οὕτως ὥστε ἓν εἶναι τὸ πᾶν, [ἂν] μὴ ὡς σωρὸς ἀλλʼ ὡς ἡ συλλαβή—ἡ δὲ συλλαβὴ οὐκ ἔστι τὰ στοιχεῖα, οὐδὲ τῷ βα ταὐτὸ τὸ β καὶ α, οὐδʼ ἡ σὰρξ πῦρ καὶ γῆ (διαλυθέντων γὰρ τὰ μὲν οὐκέτι ἔστιν, οἷον ἡ σὰρξ καὶ ἡ συλλαβή, τὰ δὲ στοιχεῖα ἔστι, καὶ τὸ πῦρ καὶ ἡ γῆ)· ἔστιν ἄρα τι ἡ συλλαβή, οὐ μόνον τὰ στοιχεῖα τὸ φωνῆεν καὶ ἄφωνον ἀλλὰ καὶ ἕτερόν τι, καὶ ἡ σὰρξ οὐ μόνον πῦρ καὶ γῆ ἢ τὸ θερμὸν καὶ ψυχρὸν ἀλλὰ καὶ ἕτερόν τι—εἰ τοίνυν ἀνάγκη κἀκεῖνο ἢ στοιχεῖον ἢ ἐκ στοιχείων εἶναι, εἰ μὲν στοιχεῖον, πάλιν ὁ αὐτὸς ἔσται λόγος (ἐκ τούτου γὰρ καὶ πυρὸς καὶ γῆς ἔσται ἡ σὰρξ καὶ ἔτι ἄλλου, ὥστʼ εἰς ἄπειρον βαδιεῖταi)· εἰ δὲ ἐκ στοιχείου, δῆλον ὅτι οὐχ ἑνὸς ἀλλὰ πλειόνων, ἢ ἐκεῖνο αὐτὸ ἔσται, ὥστε πάλιν ἐπὶ τούτου τὸν αὐτὸν ἐροῦμεν λόγον καὶ ἐπὶ τῆς σαρκὸς ἢ συλλαβῆς. δόξειε δʼ ἂν εἶναι τὶ τοῦτο καὶ οὐ στοιχεῖον, καὶ αἴτιόν γε τοῦ εἶναι τοδὶ μὲν σάρκα τοδὶ δὲ συλλαβήν· ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν ἄλλων. οὐσία δὲ ἑκάστου μὲν τοῦτο (τοῦτο γὰρ αἴτιον πρῶτον τοῦ εἶναι)—ἐπεὶ δʼ ἔνια οὐκ οὐσίαι τῶν πραγμάτων, ἀλλʼ ὅσαι οὐσίαι, κατὰ φύσιν καὶ φύσει συνεστήκασι, φανείη ἂν [καὶ] αὕτη ἡ φύσις οὐσία, ἥ ἐστιν οὐ στοιχεῖον ἀλλʼ ἀρχή—· στοιχεῖον δʼ ἐστὶν εἰς ὃ διαιρεῖται ἐνυπάρχον ὡς ὕλην, οἷον τῆς συλλαβῆς τὸ α καὶ τὸ β.
notes: The end of Book Ζ: the substance of each thing is its form, the cause of its being what it is, not a further part beside its parts. Book Η takes up the sensible substances in these terms, matter and form as potency and actuality; Book Λ goes on to the substances that are separate. For the Platonists the chapter, with its "nature which is a principle", leads from the forms in matter up toward the Forms in intellect, which they took to be the forms' causes.

paragraphs.modern: We must draw conclusions from what has been said, gather up the main points, and so bring the inquiry to its end. We have said that what we are looking for is the causes, the principles and the elements of substances. Some substances are agreed on by everyone, while some thinkers have declared others of their own. Those agreed on are the natural substances: fire, earth, water, air and the other simple bodies; then plants and their parts; animals and the parts of animals; and finally the heaven and the parts of the heaven. Some thinkers, on their own account, say that the Forms and the objects of mathematics are substances. And our arguments have brought out further substances: what it is to be, and the underlying thing. Again, in another way, the genus seems to be substance more than the species, and the universal more than the particulars; and the Forms are bound up with the universal and the genus, since they are thought to be substances by the same argument. Since what it is to be is substance, and its account is the definition, we have discussed definition and what belongs to a thing in itself. And since the definition is an account, and an account has parts, we had to consider parts too: which are parts of the substance and which are not, and whether the parts of the substance are also parts of the definition. Further, neither the universal nor the genus is substance. The Forms and the objects of mathematics we must look into later, for some say that these exist besides the sensible substances.
paragraphs.greek: ἐκ δὴ τῶν εἰρημένων συλλογίσασθαι δεῖ καὶ συναγαγόντας τὸ κεφάλαιον τέλος ἐπιθεῖναι. εἴρηται δὴ ὅτι τῶν οὐσιῶν ζητεῖται τὰ αἴτια καὶ αἱ ἀρχαὶ καὶ τὰ στοιχεῖα. οὐσίαι δὲ αἱ μὲν ὁμολογούμεναί εἰσιν ὑπὸ πάντων, περὶ δὲ ἐνίων ἰδίᾳ τινὲς ἀπεφήναντο· ὁμολογούμεναι μὲν αἱ φυσικαί, οἷον πῦρ γῆ ὕδωρ ἀὴρ καὶ τἆλλα τὰ ἁπλᾶ σώματα, ἔπειτα τὰ φυτὰ καὶ τὰ μόρια αὐτῶν, καὶ τὰ ζῷα καὶ τὰ μόρια τῶν ζῴων, καὶ τέλος ὁ οὐρανὸς καὶ τὰ μόρια τοῦ οὐρανοῦ· ἰδίᾳ δέ τινες οὐσίας λέγουσιν εἶναι τά τʼ εἴδη καὶ τὰ μαθηματικά. ἄλλας δὲ δὴ συμβαίνει ἐκ τῶν λόγων οὐσίας εἶναι, τὸ τί ἦν εἶναι καὶ τὸ ὑποκείμενον· ἔτι ἄλλως τὸ γένος μᾶλλον τῶν εἰδῶν καὶ τὸ καθόλου τῶν καθʼ ἕκαστα· τῷ δὲ καθόλου καὶ τῷ γένει καὶ αἱ ἰδέαι συνάπτουσιν (κατὰ τὸν αὐτὸν γὰρ λόγον οὐσίαι δοκοῦσιν εἶναι). ἐπεὶ δὲ τὸ τί ἦν εἶναι οὐσία, τούτου δὲ λόγος ὁ ὁρισμός, διὰ τοῦτο περὶ ὁρισμοῦ καὶ περὶ τοῦ καθʼ αὑτὸ διώρισται· ἐπεὶ δὲ ὁ ὁρισμὸς λόγος, ὁ δὲ λόγος μέρη ἔχει, ἀναγκαῖον καὶ περὶ μέρους ἦν ἰδεῖν, ποῖα τῆς οὐσίας μέρη καὶ ποῖα οὔ, καὶ εἰ ταῦτα καὶ τοῦ ὁρισμοῦ. ἔτι τοίνυν οὔτε τὸ καθόλου οὐσία οὔτε τὸ γένος· περὶ δὲ τῶν ἰδεῶν καὶ τῶν μαθηματικῶν ὕστερον σκεπτέον· παρὰ γὰρ τὰς αἰσθητὰς οὐσίας ταύτας λέγουσί τινες εἶναι.—

flags.taylor: forms and the mathematical species
flags.why: Taylor's "mathematical species" renders τὰ μαθηματικά, "the objects of mathematics", the numbers and figures that some of Plato's school set between the Forms and sensible things. The modern version says "the objects of mathematics", as throughout this work.

notes: "Later": Books Μ and Ν (XIII and XIV), on the Forms and the numbers. The summary runs over Book Ζ: the four candidates for substance (VII.3), definition and what belongs in itself (VII.4-6, 10-12), the universal and the genus (VII.13-16).

paragraphs.modern: Now let us go on to the substances that are agreed on. These are the sensible substances, and the sensible substances all have matter. The underlying thing is substance: in one way the matter (by matter I mean what is not a this in actuality, but is a this in potency); in another way the account and the form, which, being a this, is separable in account; and third, what is made of these, which alone comes to be and perishes, and is separable without qualification. For of the substances that answer to the account, some are separable and some are not.
paragraphs.greek: νῦν δὲ περὶ τῶν ὁμολογουμένων οὐσιῶν ἐπέλθωμεν. αὗται δʼ εἰσὶν αἱ αἰσθηταί· αἱ δʼ αἰσθηταὶ οὐσίαι πᾶσαι ὕλην ἔχουσιν. ἔστι δʼ οὐσία τὸ ὑποκείμενον, ἄλλως μὲν ἡ ὕλη (ὕλην δὲ λέγω ἣ μὴ τόδε τι οὖσα ἐνεργείᾳ δυνάμει ἐστὶ τόδε τι), ἄλλως δʼ ὁ λόγος καὶ ἡ μορφή, ὃ τόδε τι ὂν τῷ λόγῳ χωριστόν ἐστιν· τρίτον δὲ τὸ ἐκ τούτων, οὗ γένεσις μόνου καὶ φθορά ἐστι, καὶ χωριστὸν ἁπλῶς· τῶν γὰρ κατὰ τὸν λόγον οὐσιῶν αἱ μὲν αἱ δʼ οὔ.
notes: The three ways of being substance are those of Book Ζ (VII.3): matter, form and the compound. "Separable in account": the form can be stated by itself, though it does not exist apart from its matter; the compound, the man or the horse, exists apart without qualification.

paragraphs.modern: That matter too is substance is plain. In all the changes between opposites there is something that underlies the changes: in change of place, what is now here and later somewhere else; in growth, what is now of this size and later smaller or larger; in alteration, what is now healthy and later sick. And likewise in change of substance there is something that is now coming to be and later perishing, and that now underlies as a this, and later underlies as by privation. The other changes follow on this one; but this one does not follow on one or two of the others. For it is not necessary that if something has matter for change of place, it should also have matter for coming to be and perishing. The difference between coming to be without qualification and coming to be in a certain respect has been stated in the works on nature.
paragraphs.greek: ὅτι δʼ ἐστὶν οὐσία καὶ ἡ ὕλη, δῆλον· ἐν πάσαις γὰρ ταῖς ἀντικειμέναις μεταβολαῖς ἐστί τι τὸ ὑποκείμενον ταῖς μεταβολαῖς, οἷον κατὰ τόπον τὸ νῦν μὲν ἐνταῦθα πάλιν δʼ ἄλλοθι, καὶ κατʼ αὔξησιν ὃ νῦν μὲν τηλικόνδε πάλιν δʼ ἔλαττον ἢ μεῖζον, καὶ κατʼ ἀλλοίωσιν ὃ νῦν μὲν ὑγιὲς πάλιν δὲ κάμνον· ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ κατʼ οὐσίαν ὃ νῦν μὲν ἐν γενέσει πάλιν δʼ ἐν φθορᾷ, καὶ νῦν μὲν ὑποκείμενον ὡς τόδε τι πάλιν δʼ ὑποκείμενον ὡς κατὰ στέρησιν. καὶ ἀκολουθοῦσι δὴ ταύτῃ αἱ ἄλλαι μεταβολαί, τῶν δʼ ἄλλων ἢ μιᾷ ἢ δυοῖν αὕτη οὐκ ἀκολουθεῖ· οὐ γὰρ ἀνάγκη, εἴ τι ὕλην ἔχει τοπικήν, τοῦτο καὶ γεννητὴν καὶ φθαρτὴν ἔχειν. τίς μὲν οὖν διαφορὰ τοῦ ἁπλῶς γίγνεσθαι καὶ μὴ ἁπλῶς, ἐν τοῖς φυσικοῖς εἴρηται.

flags.taylor: according to internal change, he who is now well
flags.why: Taylor's "internal change" renders ἀλλοίωσις, "alteration", change of quality, as from healthy to sick; Ross says "alteration", as the modern version does. Aristotle's four kinds of change are of place, of size (growth and shrinking), of quality and of substance (coming to be and perishing).

flags.taylor: underlies it as the privation of positive character
flags.why: The Greek says only "underlies as by privation" (ὡς κατὰ στέρησιν); Ross's "of positive character" spells out what the thing is deprived of, its form. The modern version keeps the Greek's bare words.

notes: "The works on nature": the Physics (V.1, 225a12-20) and On Coming to Be and Perishing (I.2-3, 317a17-319b5). The heavenly bodies, which move in place but do not come to be or perish, have matter for motion only (VIII.4).

paragraphs.modern: Since the substance that is as underlying thing and as matter is agreed on, and this is substance in potency, it remains to say what the substance of sensible things is as actuality. Democritus seems to think there are three differences between things: the underlying body, the matter, is one and the same, but things differ in rhythm, that is, shape; in turning, that is, position; or in contact, that is, order. But there appear to be many differences. Some things are spoken of by the way their matter is put together, as things made by blending, like honey-water; others by binding, like a bundle; others by glue, like a book; others by nails, like a box; others by more than one of these. Others again by position, like the threshold and the lintel (these differ by lying in a certain way); others by time, like dinner and breakfast; others by place, like the winds; others by the affections of sensible things, like hardness and softness, density and rarity, dryness and wetness; some by some of these, others by all of them; and in general some by excess and some by deficiency. So it is clear that "is" too is said in just as many ways. A threshold is, because it lies thus, and its being means its lying thus; and being ice means being solidified thus. The being of some things will be defined by all of these: some of their parts are mixed, some blended, some bound, some solidified, and some use the other differences, like the hand or the foot. We must grasp, then, the kinds of the differences (for these will be the principles of being): those of the more and the less, for instance, or of the dense and the rare, and the other such, for all these are excess and deficiency. Whatever differs by shape, or by smoothness and roughness, differs by the straight and the curved. For other things their being will be their being mixed, and their not being the opposite.
paragraphs.greek: ἐπεὶ δʼ ἡ μὲν ὡς ὑποκειμένη καὶ ὡς ὕλη οὐσία ὁμολογεῖται, αὕτη δʼ ἐστὶν ἡ δυνάμει, λοιπὸν τὴν ὡς ἐνέργειαν οὐσίαν τῶν αἰσθητῶν εἰπεῖν τίς ἐστιν. Δημόκριτος μὲν οὖν τρεῖς διαφορὰς ἔοικεν οἰομένῳ εἶναι (τὸ μὲν γὰρ ὑποκείμενον σῶμα, τὴν ὕλην, ἓν καὶ ταὐτόν, διαφέρειν δὲ ἢ ῥυσμῷ, ὅ ἐστι σχῆμα, ἢ τροπῇ, ὅ ἐστι θέσις, ἢ διαθιγῇ, ὅ ἐστι τάξις)· φαίνονται δὲ πολλαὶ διαφοραὶ οὖσαι, οἷον τὰ μὲν συνθέσει λέγεται τῆς ὕλης, ὥσπερ ὅσα κράσει καθάπερ μελίκρατον, τὰ δὲ δεσμῷ οἷον φάκελος, τὰ δὲ κόλλῃ οἷον βιβλίον, τὰ δὲ γόμφῳ οἷον κιβώτιον, τὰ δὲ πλείοσι τούτων, τὰ δὲ θέσει οἷον οὐδὸς καὶ ὑπέρθυρον (ταῦτα γὰρ τῷ κεῖσθαί πως διαφέρει), τὰ δὲ χρόνῳ οἷον δεῖπνον καὶ ἄριστον, τὰ δὲ τόπῳ οἷον τὰ πνεύματα· τὰ δὲ τοῖς τῶν αἰσθητῶν πάθεσιν οἷον σκληρότητι καὶ μαλακότητι, καὶ πυκνότητι καὶ ἀραιότητι, καὶ ξηρότητι καὶ ὑγρότητι, καὶ τὰ μὲν ἐνίοις τούτων τὰ δὲ πᾶσι τούτοις, καὶ ὅλως τὰ μὲν ὑπεροχῇ τὰ δὲ ἐλλείψει. ὥστε δῆλον ὅτι καὶ τὸ ἔστι τοσαυταχῶς λέγεται· οὐδὸς γὰρ ἔστιν ὅτι οὕτως κεῖται, καὶ τὸ εἶναι τὸ οὕτως αὐτὸ κεῖσθαι σημαίνει, καὶ τὸ κρύσταλλον εἶναι τὸ οὕτω πεπυκνῶσθαι. ἐνίων δὲ τὸ εἶναι καὶ πᾶσι τούτοις ὁρισθήσεται, τῷ τὰ μὲν μεμῖχθαι, τὰ δὲ κεκρᾶσθαι, τὰ δὲ δεδέσθαι, τὰ δὲ πεπυκνῶσθαι, τὰ δὲ ταῖς ἄλλαις διαφοραῖς κεχρῆσθαι, ὥσπερ χεὶρ ἢ πούς. ληπτέα οὖν τὰ γένη τῶν διαφορῶν (αὗται γὰρ ἀρχαὶ ἔσονται τοῦ εἶναι), οἷον τὰ τῷ μᾶλλον καὶ ἧττον ἢ πυκνῷ καὶ μανῷ καὶ τοῖς ἄλλοις τοῖς τοιούτοις· πάντα γὰρ ταῦτα ὑπεροχὴ καὶ ἔλλειψίς ἐστιν. εἰ δέ τι σχήματι ἢ λειότητι καὶ τραχύτητι, πάντα εὐθεῖ καὶ καμπύλῳ. τοῖς δὲ τὸ εἶναι τὸ μεμῖχθαι ἔσται, ἀντικειμένως δὲ τὸ μὴ εἶναι.

flags.taylor: or by trope which is position
flags.why: Taylor's "trope" and "ryfm" (as the scan has it) and "diathige" carry over Democritus' own words, τροπή ("turning"), ῥυσμός ("rhythm", the Abderite form of ῥυθμός) and διαθιγή ("touching"), which Aristotle glosses as position, shape and order. Ross translates them "turning", "rhythm" and "inter-contact"; the modern version gives Democritus' words and Aristotle's glosses both. Book Α (I.4, 985b13-19) explains them with the letters A and N, AN and NA, Z and N.

flags.taylor: some things are from transcendency, others from deficiency
flags.why: Taylor's "transcendency" renders ὑπεροχή, "excess", "exceeding"; the word has nothing of the later sense of transcending. The modern version says "excess".

paragraphs.modern: It is plain from this, then, that if the substance is the cause of each thing's being, it is among these differences that we must look for the cause of the being of each of these things. None of them is substance, not even when coupled with the matter; yet in each there is something analogous. And as in substances what is predicated of the matter is the actuality itself, so in the other definitions too it is this most of all. If we had to define a threshold, for instance, we would say "wood or stone lying thus", and a house "bricks and timbers lying thus" (or in some cases we would add that for the sake of which as well); if ice, "water frozen" or "solidified thus"; a concord is "such and such a blending of high and low"; and in the same way with the rest.
paragraphs.greek: φανερὸν δὴ ἐκ τούτων ὅτι εἴπερ ἡ οὐσία αἰτία τοῦ εἶναι ἕκαστον, ὅτι ἐν τούτοις ζητητέον τί τὸ αἴτιον τοῦ εἶναι τούτων ἕκαστον. οὐσία μὲν οὖν οὐδὲν τούτων οὐδὲ συνδυαζόμενον, ὅμως δὲ τὸ ἀνάλογον ἐν ἑκάστῳ· καὶ ὡς ἐν ταῖς οὐσίαις τὸ τῆς ὕλης κατηγορούμενον αὐτὴ ἡ ἐνέργεια, καὶ ἐν τοῖς ἄλλοις ὁρισμοῖς μάλιστα. οἷον εἰ οὐδὸν δέοι ὁρίσασθαι, ξύλον ἢ λίθον ὡδὶ κείμενον ἐροῦμεν, καὶ οἰκίαν πλίνθους καὶ ξύλα ὡδὶ κείμενα (ἢ ἔτι καὶ τὸ οὗ ἕνεκα ἐπʼ ἐνίων ἔστιν), εἰ δὲ κρύσταλλον, ὕδωρ πεπηγὸς ἢ πεπυκνωμένον ὡδί· συμφωνία δὲ ὀξέος καὶ βαρέος μῖξις τοιαδί· τὸν αὐτὸν δὲ τρόπον καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν ἄλλων.

flags.taylor: that which is predicated of matter is energy itself
flags.why: Taylor's "energy" renders ἐνέργεια, "actuality", "being at work", the word this book and the next turn on; Ross says "actuality", as the modern version does throughout this work. Taylor uses "energy" in its old sense of activity, which is the Greek's: from ἔργον, "work".

flags.taylor: it is what most resembles full actuality
flags.why: The Greek says only "and in the other definitions most of all" (καὶ ἐν τοῖς ἄλλοις ὁρισμοῖς μάλιστα): what is predicated of the matter is the actuality most of all, or the actuality is so predicated most of all in the other definitions. Ross's "what most resembles full actuality" is his reading of the compressed line.

notes: "Concord" (συμφωνία): a consonant interval, such as the octave, which the Pythagoreans defined by a ratio of high and low; Ross says "harmony", Taylor "symphony". Plato's Timaeus (80a-b) and Philebus (17c-d, 26a) speak of the high and the low blended by limit.

paragraphs.modern: It is plain from this, then, that the actuality is different for different matter, and so is the account: for some it is the putting together, for others the mixing, for others another of those we have named. That is why, of those who define, those who say what a house is by saying "stones, bricks, timbers" are speaking of the house in potency, for these are its matter; those who put forward "a shelter for goods and bodies", or something else of the kind, are speaking of the actuality; and those who combine the two are speaking of the third substance, the one made of these. For the account through the differences seems to be of the form and the actuality, and the one from the constituents rather of the matter. Likewise with the kind of definitions Archytas used to accept, for they are of the two together. What is still weather? Rest in a mass of air: the air is the matter, and the rest is the actuality and substance. What is calm? Smoothness of sea: the underlying thing, as matter, is the sea, and the actuality and form is the smoothness. It is plain from what has been said, then, what the sensible substance is and how it is: one as matter, another as form and actuality, and the third the one made of these.
paragraphs.greek: φανερὸν δὴ ἐκ τούτων ὅτι ἡ ἐνέργεια ἄλλη ἄλλης ὕλης καὶ ὁ λόγος· τῶν μὲν γὰρ ἡ σύνθεσις τῶν δʼ ἡ μῖξις τῶν δὲ ἄλλο τι τῶν εἰρημένων. διὸ τῶν ὁριζομένων οἱ μὲν λέγοντες τί ἐστιν οἰκία, ὅτι λίθοι πλίνθοι ξύλα, τὴν δυνάμει οἰκίαν λέγουσιν, ὕλη γὰρ ταῦτα· οἱ δὲ ἀγγεῖον σκεπαστικὸν χρημάτων καὶ σωμάτων ἤ τι ἄλλο τοιοῦτον προτιθέντες, τὴν ἐνέργειαν λέγουσιν· οἱ δʼ ἄμφω ταῦτα συντιθέντες τὴν τρίτην καὶ τὴν ἐκ τούτων οὐσίαν (ἔοικε γὰρ ὁ μὲν διὰ τῶν διαφορῶν λόγος τοῦ εἴδους καὶ τῆς ἐνεργείας εἶναι, ὁ δʼ ἐκ τῶν ἐνυπαρχόντων τῆς ὕλης μᾶλλον)· ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ οἵους Ἀρχύτας ἀπεδέχετο ὅρους· τοῦ συνάμφω γάρ εἰσιν. οἷον τί ἐστι νηνεμία; ἠρεμία ἐν πλήθει ἀέρος· ὕλη μὲν γὰρ ὁ ἀήρ, ἐνέργεια δὲ καὶ οὐσία ἡ ἠρεμία. τί ἐστι γαλήνη; ὁμαλότης θαλάττης· τὸ μὲν ὑποκείμενον ὡς ὕλη ἡ θάλαττα, ἡ δὲ ἐνέργεια καὶ ἡ μορφὴ ἡ ὁμαλότης. φανερὸν δὴ ἐκ τῶν εἰρημένων τίς ἡ αἰσθητὴ οὐσία ἐστὶ καὶ πῶς· ἡ μὲν γὰρ ὡς ὕλη, ἡ δʼ ὡς μορφὴ καὶ ἐνέργεια, ἡ δὲ τρίτη ἡ ἐκ τούτων.
notes: Archytas of Tarentum, the Pythagorean mathematician and statesman, Plato's friend (the Seventh Letter, 338c-339b, 350a-b). His definitions join a matter (air, sea) to a form (rest, smoothness), and so state the compound.
"Shelter" (σκέπασμα): the house as defined by its use, which is its form; De Anima (I.1, 403b3-7) sets the same three definitions of a house side by side.

paragraphs.modern: We must not overlook that it is sometimes unclear whether a name signifies the compound substance or the actuality and form. Does "house", for instance, signify the common thing, "a shelter made of bricks and stones lying thus", or the actuality and form, "a shelter"? Is a line "a dyad in length" or "a dyad"? Is an animal "a soul in a body" or "a soul"? For the soul is the substance and actuality of a certain body. "Animal" might apply to both, not as said by one account, but as related to one thing. This makes a difference for another purpose, but none for the inquiry into sensible substance; for what it is to be belongs to the form and the actuality. Soul and being soul are the same, but being man and man are not the same, unless the soul too is to be called man; and so in one way they are the same, and in another not.
paragraphs.greek: δεῖ δὲ μὴ ἀγνοεῖν ὅτι ἐνίοτε λανθάνει πότερον σημαίνει τὸ ὄνομα τὴν σύνθετον οὐσίαν ἢ τὴν ἐνέργειαν καὶ τὴν μορφήν, οἷον ἡ οἰκία πότερον σημεῖον τοῦ κοινοῦ ὅτι σκέπασμα ἐκ πλίνθων καὶ λίθων ὡδὶ κειμένων, ἢ τῆς ἐνεργείας καὶ τοῦ εἴδους ὅτι σκέπασμα, καὶ γραμμὴ πότερον δυὰς ἐν μήκει ἢ [ὅτι] δυάς, καὶ ζῷον πότερον ψυχὴ ἐν σώματι ἢ ψυχή· αὕτη γὰρ οὐσία καὶ ἐνέργεια σώματός τινος. εἴη δʼ ἂν καὶ ἐπʼ ἀμφοτέροις τὸ ζῷον, οὐχ ὡς ἑνὶ λόγῳ λεγόμενον ἀλλʼ ὡς πρὸς ἕν. ἀλλὰ ταῦτα πρὸς μέν τι ἄλλο διαφέρει, πρὸς δὲ τὴν ζήτησιν τῆς οὐσίας τῆς αἰσθητῆς οὐδέν· τὸ γὰρ τί ἦν εἶναι τῷ εἴδει καὶ τῇ ἐνεργείᾳ ὑπάρχει. ψυχὴ μὲν γὰρ καὶ ψυχῇ εἶναι ταὐτόν, ἀνθρώπῳ δὲ καὶ ἄνθρωπος οὐ ταὐτόν, εἰ μὴ καὶ ἡ ψυχὴ ἄνθρωπος λεχθήσεται· οὕτω δὲ τινὶ μὲν τινὶ δʼ οὔ.—

flags.taylor: whether it is a duad in length
flags.why: Taylor's "duad" is δυάς, "dyad", "two", which the modern version says, as throughout this work. The line as "a dyad in length" is the Academy's: Book Ζ (VII.11, 1036b12-17) reports that some reduce the line to "two" itself, as its form, and Book Ν reports Plato's derivation of lines from the great and the small. Ross says "twoness".

notes: "The soul is the substance and actuality of a certain body": the definition of On the Soul (II.1, 412a19-28), the soul as the first actuality of a natural body that has life in potency. The Platonists accepted it for the soul as the body's form, and held that the rational soul is also separable (Plotinus IV.7.8).

paragraphs.modern: When we look, a syllable does not turn out to be its letters plus their putting together, nor a house bricks plus their putting together. And this is right: for the putting together or the mixing is not made of the things whose putting together or mixing it is. Likewise with all the rest: if a threshold is a threshold by position, the position is not made of the threshold, but rather the threshold of it. Nor is man animal plus two-footed: there must be something besides these, if these are matter, which is neither an element nor made of an element, but the substance, which people leave out when they state the matter. If, then, this is the cause of being, and the substance, they would not be stating the substance itself. (This must either be eternal, or perishable without perishing, and have come to be without coming to be. It has been shown and made clear elsewhere that no one makes or begets the form: it is this that is made, and what comes to be is the thing made of these. Whether the substances of perishable things are separable is not yet at all clear; except that for some it is clearly impossible, for those that cannot be besides the particular ones, such as a house or a utensil. Perhaps, indeed, neither these things themselves nor any of the other things not put together by nature are substances; for one might set down nature alone as the substance in perishable things.)
paragraphs.greek: οὐ φαίνεται δὴ ζητοῦσιν ἡ συλλαβὴ ἐκ τῶν στοιχείων οὖσα καὶ συνθέσεως, οὐδʼ ἡ οἰκία πλίνθοι τε καὶ σύνθεσις. καὶ τοῦτο ὀρθῶς· οὐ γάρ ἐστιν ἡ σύνθεσις οὐδʼ ἡ μῖξις ἐκ τούτων ὧν ἐστὶ σύνθεσις ἢ μῖξις. ὁμοίως δὲ οὐδὲ τῶν ἄλλων οὐθέν, οἷον εἰ ὁ οὐδὸς θέσει, οὐκ ἐκ τοῦ οὐδοῦ ἡ θέσις ἀλλὰ μᾶλλον οὗτος ἐξ ἐκείνης. οὐδὲ δὴ ὁ ἄνθρωπός ἐστι τὸ ζῷον καὶ δίπουν, ἀλλά τι δεῖ εἶναι ὃ παρὰ ταῦτά ἐστιν, εἰ ταῦθʼ ὕλη, οὔτε δὲ στοιχεῖον οὔτʼ ἐκ στοιχείου, ἀλλʼ ἡ οὐσία· ὃ ἐξαιροῦντες τὴν ὕλην λέγουσιν. εἰ οὖν τοῦτʼ αἴτιον τοῦ εἶναι, καὶ οὐσία τοῦτο, αὐτὴν ἂν τὴν οὐσίαν οὐ λέγοιεν. (ἀνάγκη δὴ ταύτην ἢ ἀΐδιον εἶναι ἢ φθαρτὴν ἄνευ τοῦ φθείρεσθαι καὶ γεγονέναι ἄνευ τοῦ γίγνεσθαι. δέδεικται δὲ καὶ δεδήλωται ἐν ἄλλοις ὅτι τὸ εἶδος οὐθεὶς ποιεῖ οὐδὲ γεννᾷ, ἀλλὰ ποιεῖται τόδε, γίγνεται δὲ τὸ ἐκ τούτων. εἰ δʼ εἰσὶ τῶν φθαρτῶν αἱ οὐσίαι χωρισταί, οὐδέν πω δῆλον· πλὴν ὅτι γʼ ἐνίων οὐκ ἐνδέχεται δῆλον, ὅσα μὴ οἷόν τε παρὰ τὰ τινὰ εἶναι, οἷον οἰκίαν ἢ σκεῦος. ἴσως μὲν οὖν οὐδʼ οὐσίαι εἰσὶν οὔτʼ αὐτὰ ταῦτα οὔτε τι τῶν ἄλλων ὅσα μὴ φύσει συνέστηκεν· τὴν γὰρ φύσιν μόνην ἄν τις θείη τὴν ἐν τοῖς φθαρτοῖς οὐσίαν.)
notes: "Shown elsewhere": Book Ζ (VII.8, 1033a24-b19): no one makes the form, the sphere, but this bronze sphere. The form "perishable without perishing": it is and then is not, without a process of perishing, as the line has it at VIII.5.

"Nature alone" as substance among perishable things: Aristotle leaves open whether artefacts, houses and utensils, have substances at all. The Platonists, too, posited Forms of natural things and not of artefacts (Book Α, I.9, 991b6-7; Proclus on the Parmenides, Book III), though Plato's Republic (596b) speaks of the Form of the bed.

paragraphs.modern: So the puzzle that the followers of Antisthenes, and other such uneducated people, raised has a certain point. They said that it is not possible to define what a thing is (a definition, they said, is a long rigmarole), but it is possible to teach what sort of thing it is: of silver, for instance, one cannot say what it is, but one can say that it is like tin. So there is a kind of substance of which there can be a definition and an account: the compound, whether it is sensible or intelligible. But the first things it is made of cannot be defined, if indeed the defining account signifies something of something, and one part must be as matter and the other as form.
paragraphs.greek: ὥστε ἡ ἀπορία ἣν οἱ Ἀντισθένειοι καὶ οἱ οὕτως ἀπαίδευτοι ἠπόρουν ἔχει τινὰ καιρόν, ὅτι οὐκ ἔστι τὸ τί ἔστιν ὁρίσασθαι (τὸν γὰρ ὅρον λόγον εἶναι μακρόν), ἀλλὰ ποῖον μέν τί ἐστιν ἐνδέχεται καὶ διδάξαι, ὥσπερ ἄργυρον, τί μέν ἐστιν οὔ, ὅτι δʼ οἷον καττίτερος· ὥστʼ οὐσίας ἔστι μὲν ἧς ἐνδέχεται εἶναι ὅρον καὶ λόγον, οἷον τῆς συνθέτου, ἐάν τε αἰσθητὴ ἐάν τε νοητὴ ᾖ· ἐξ ὧν δʼ αὕτη πρώτων, οὐκέτι, εἴπερ τὶ κατὰ τινὸς σημαίνει ὁ λόγος ὁ ὁριστικὸς καὶ δεῖ τὸ μὲν ὥσπερ ὕλην εἶναι τὸ δὲ ὡς μορφήν.—

flags.taylor: may now be opportunely solved
flags.why: The Greek says that the puzzle "has a certain timeliness" (ἔχει τινὰ καιρόν): it has a point, it is apt. Taylor makes Aristotle say that the puzzle "may now be opportunely solved", which is not in the Greek. Ross's English has lost words in the scan here; the modern version follows the Greek.

flags.taylor: the definition so called is a
flags.why: Ross's "the definition so called is a 'long formula'" renders τὸν γὰρ ὅρον λόγον εἶναι μακρόν, "for the definition is a long account", that is, a long-winded speech, a rigmarole, as Ross's footnote says; Book Ν (1091a8) uses the phrase with the same scorn. The modern version says "a long rigmarole".

flags.taylor: whether it be the object of sense or of reason
flags.why: Ross's "object of reason" renders νοητή, "intelligible": the compound grasped by thought, not by the senses, as the objects of mathematics are. The modern version says "intelligible", as for νοητόν throughout this work; chapter 6 speaks of "intelligible matter".

notes: Antisthenes, a follower of Socrates, held that one can say of a thing only its own name, so that there is no contradiction and no definition (Book Δ, V.29, 1024b32-34). Plato's Theaetetus (201e-202c), in Socrates' "dream", gives a theory like his: the first elements have no account and can only be named. The Platonists took the dream as the doctrine that the simple is known not by account but by intellect.

paragraphs.modern: It is plain too why, if substances are in some way numbers, they are so in this way, and not, as some say, as numbers of units. For a definition is a kind of number: it is divisible, and into indivisible parts (for accounts are not unlimited), and number is of this kind. And as, when anything of which a number consists is taken away from it or added to it, it is no longer the same number but a different one, even if the least thing is taken away or added, so the definition and what it is to be will no longer be the same if anything is taken away or added. And the number must have something by which it is one, which these people cannot say, if it is one (for either it is not one, but like a heap, or, if it is, they must say what makes one out of many); and the definition is one, but likewise they cannot say what makes it one. This happens with reason, for the same account applies; and substance is one in the way we have said, not, as some say, as being a kind of unit or point, but each is an actuality and a certain nature. And as number does not admit of the more and the less, neither does substance as form; if any substance does, it is the one with matter. Let this be enough, then, on the coming to be and perishing of what are called substances, how it is possible and how impossible, and on the reduction of things to number.
paragraphs.greek: φανερὸν δὲ καὶ διότι, εἴπερ εἰσί πως ἀριθμοὶ αἱ οὐσίαι, οὕτως εἰσὶ καὶ οὐχ ὥς τινες λέγουσι μονάδων· ὅ τε γὰρ ὁρισμὸς ἀριθμός τις· διαιρετός τε γὰρ καὶ εἰς ἀδιαίρετα (οὐ γὰρ ἄπειροι οἱ λόγοι), καὶ ὁ ἀριθμὸς δὲ τοιοῦτον. καὶ ὥσπερ οὐδʼ ἀπʼ ἀριθμοῦ ἀφαιρεθέντος τινὸς ἢ προστεθέντος ἐξ ὧν ὁ ἀριθμός ἐστιν, οὐκέτι ὁ αὐτὸς ἀριθμός ἐστιν ἀλλʼ ἕτερος, κἂν τοὐλάχιστον ἀφαιρεθῇ ἢ προστεθῇ, οὕτως οὐδὲ ὁ ὁρισμὸς οὐδὲ τὸ τί ἦν εἶναι οὐκέτι ἔσται ἀφαιρεθέντος τινὸς ἢ προστεθέντος. καὶ τὸν ἀριθμὸν δεῖ εἶναί τι ᾧ εἷς, ὃ νῦν οὐκ ἔχουσι λέγειν τίνι εἷς, εἴπερ ἐστὶν εἷς (ἢ γὰρ οὐκ ἔστιν ἀλλʼ οἷον σωρός, ἢ εἴπερ ἐστί, λεκτέον τί τὸ ποιοῦν ἓν ἐκ πολλῶν)· καὶ ὁ ὁρισμὸς εἷς ἐστίν, ὁμοίως δὲ οὐδὲ τοῦτον ἔχουσι λέγειν. καὶ τοῦτο εἰκότως συμβαίνει· τοῦ αὐτοῦ γὰρ λόγου, καὶ ἡ οὐσία ἓν οὕτως, ἀλλʼ οὐχ ὡς λέγουσί τινες οἷον μονάς τις οὖσα ἢ στιγμή, ἀλλʼ ἐντελέχεια καὶ φύσις τις ἑκάστη. καὶ ὥσπερ οὐδὲ ὁ ἀριθμὸς ἔχει τὸ μᾶλλον καὶ ἧττον, οὐδʼ ἡ κατὰ τὸ εἶδος οὐσία, ἀλλʼ εἴπερ, ἡ μετὰ τῆς ὕλης. περὶ μὲν οὖν γενέσεως καὶ φθορᾶς τῶν λεγομένων οὐσιῶν, πῶς τʼ ἐνδέχεται καὶ πῶς ἀδύνατον, καὶ περὶ τῆς εἰς τὸν ἀριθμὸν ἀναγωγῆς, ἔστω μέχρι τούτων διωρισμένον.

flags.taylor: each is a complete reality and a definite nature
flags.why: Ross's "complete reality" renders ἐντελέχεια, "actuality", as in Book Ζ (VII.13); Taylor says "energy". The modern version says "actuality", as everywhere in this work.

notes: "As some say": the Pythagoreans and those of Plato's school who made substances numbers built of units. Aristotle's answer: a substance is one as a definition is, by its form, not as a sum of units; the question what makes a number one, and not a heap, comes back in Book Μ (XIII.8) and Book Ν. Proclus (Elements of Theology, props. 1-6) begins from the same question, how every manifold shares in the one.

paragraphs.modern: About the material substance we must not overlook that, even if all things come from the same first cause, or from the same things as first causes, and the same matter is the starting point of what comes to be, there is still a matter proper to each thing. The proper matter of phlegm, for instance, is the sweet or the fat, and of bile the bitter or something else; though perhaps these come from the same thing. There come to be several matters of the same thing when one matter is the matter of the other: phlegm, for instance, comes from the fat and from the sweet, if the fat comes from the sweet; and from bile, by the bile's being broken down into its first matter. For one thing comes from another in two ways: either as a further stage along the way, or by the other's being broken down into its principle. When the matter is one, different things can come to be through the moving cause: from wood, for instance, both a box and a bed. But some different things must have different matter: a saw, for instance, could not come to be from wood, nor is this in the power of the moving cause, for it will not make a saw from wool or from wood. If, after all, the same thing can be made from other matter, clearly the art, the principle as mover, is the same; for if both the matter and the mover were different, so would be what has come to be.
paragraphs.greek: περὶ δὲ τῆς ὑλικῆς οὐσίας δεῖ μὴ λανθάνειν ὅτι εἰ καὶ ἐκ τοῦ αὐτοῦ πάντα πρώτου ἢ τῶν αὐτῶν ὡς πρώτων καὶ ἡ αὐτὴ ὕλη ὡς ἀρχὴ τοῖς γιγνομένοις, ὅμως ἔστι τις οἰκεία ἑκάστου, οἷον φλέγματος [ἐστι πρώτη ὕλη] τὰ γλυκέα ἢ λιπαρά, χολῆς δὲ τὰ πικρὰ ἢ ἄλλʼ ἄττα· ἴσως δὲ ταῦτα ἐκ τοῦ αὐτοῦ. γίγνονται δὲ πλείους ὗλαι τοῦ αὐτοῦ ὅταν θατέρου ἡ ἑτέρα ᾖ, οἷον φλέγμα ἐκ λιπαροῦ καὶ γλυκέος εἰ τὸ λιπαρὸν ἐκ τοῦ γλυκέος, ἐκ δὲ χολῆς τῷ ἀναλύεσθαι εἰς τὴν πρώτην ὕλην τὴν χολήν. διχῶς γὰρ τόδʼ ἐκ τοῦδε, ἢ ὅτι πρὸ ὁδοῦ ἔσται ἢ ὅτι ἀναλυθέντος εἰς τὴν ἀρχήν. ἐνδέχεται δὲ μιᾶς τῆς ὕλης οὔσης ἕτερα γίγνεσθαι διὰ τὴν κινοῦσαν αἰτίαν, οἷον ἐκ ξύλου καὶ κιβωτὸς καὶ κλίνη. ἐνίων δʼ ἑτέρα ἡ ὕλη ἐξ ἀνάγκης ἑτέρων ὄντων, οἷον πρίων οὐκ ἂν γένοιτο ἐκ ξύλου, οὐδʼ ἐπὶ τῇ κινούσῃ αἰτίᾳ τοῦτο· οὐ γὰρ ποιήσει πρίονα ἐξ ἐρίου ἢ ξύλου. εἰ δʼ ἄρα τὸ αὐτὸ ἐνδέχεται ἐξ ἄλλης ὕλης ποιῆσαι, δῆλον ὅτι ἡ τέχνη καὶ ἡ ἀρχὴ ἡ ὡς κινοῦσα ἡ αὐτή· εἰ γὰρ καὶ ἡ ὕλη ἑτέρα καὶ τὸ κινοῦν, καὶ τὸ γεγονός.—

flags.taylor: either by progression, or analyfation
flags.why: Taylor's "progression" renders πρὸ ὁδοῦ, "further along the road": one thing comes from another as a later stage of the way it develops, as the fat from the sweet. The scan of Ross has lost a line here, between "analysed" and "things may be produced"; the modern version follows the Greek.

paragraphs.modern: When one looks for the cause, then, since causes are spoken of in several ways, one must state all the possible causes. What is the cause of a man as matter? The menses, surely. What, as mover? The seed, surely. What, as form? What it is to be. What, as that for the sake of which? The end. (But perhaps these last two are the same.) And one must state the nearest causes. What is the matter? Not fire or earth, but the matter proper to the thing.
paragraphs.greek: ὅταν δή τις ζητῇ τὸ αἴτιον, ἐπεὶ πλεοναχῶς τὰ αἴτια λέγεται, πάσας δεῖ λέγειν τὰς ἐνδεχομένας αἰτίας. οἷον ἀνθρώπου τίς αἰτία ὡς ὕλη; ἆρα τὰ καταμήνια; τί δʼ ὡς κινοῦν; ἆρα τὸ σπέρμα; τί δʼ ὡς τὸ εἶδος; τὸ τί ἦν εἶναι. τί δʼ ὡς οὗ ἕνεκα; τὸ τέλος. ἴσως δὲ ταῦτα ἄμφω τὸ αὐτό. δεῖ δὲ τὰ ἐγγύτατα αἴτια λέγειν. τίς ἡ ὕλη; μὴ πῦρ ἢ γῆν ἀλλὰ τὴν ἴδιον.

flags.taylor: The final cause? His end
flags.why: Ross names the causes with the later schools' words, "material", "moving", "formal" and "final"; the Greek asks only what the cause is "as matter", "as mover", "as form" and "as that for the sake of which". The modern version keeps the Greek's plainer words, as in Book Ζ (VII.17).

notes: The four causes of a man are those of the Generation of Animals (I.1, 715a4-11; I.20-21): the menses as matter, the seed as the source of motion, the form and the end, which are one, since the end of coming to be is the form. "Perhaps the same": the form and the end often coincide (Physics II.7, 198a24-27), since the end of coming to be is to have the form.

paragraphs.modern: With natural substances that come to be, one must proceed in this way, if one is to proceed rightly, since these are the causes and this is their number, and one must know the causes. But with natural substances that are eternal there is another account. For perhaps some have no matter, or not matter of this kind, but only matter that can move in place. Nor do the things that are by nature but are not substances have matter: the underlying thing is the substance. What is the cause of an eclipse, for instance? What is its matter? There is none: the moon is what undergoes it. What is the cause as what moves and destroys the light? The earth. The cause as that for the sake of which perhaps does not exist. The cause as form is the account; but this is unclear unless the account includes the cause. What is an eclipse? Privation of light. But if one adds "by the earth's coming in between", this is the account with the cause. With sleep it is unclear what it is that first undergoes it. The animal, one says? Yes, but the animal in virtue of what, and what first? The heart, or something else. Then, by what is it produced? Then, what is the affection, the affection of that part and not of the whole? That it is such and such an immobility? Yes, but this belongs to it by the first part's undergoing what?
paragraphs.greek: περὶ μὲν οὖν τὰς φυσικὰς οὐσίας καὶ γενητὰς ἀνάγκη οὕτω μετιέναι εἴ τις μέτεισιν ὀρθῶς, εἴπερ ἄρα αἴτιά τε ταῦτα καὶ τοσαῦτα καὶ δεῖ τὰ αἴτια γνωρίζειν· ἐπὶ δὲ τῶν φυσικῶν μὲν ἀϊδίων δὲ οὐσιῶν ἄλλος λόγος. ἴσως γὰρ ἔνια οὐκ ἔχει ὕλην, ἢ οὐ τοιαύτην ἀλλὰ μόνον κατὰ τόπον κινητήν. οὐδʼ ὅσα δὴ φύσει μέν, μὴ οὐσίαι δέ, οὐκ ἔστι τούτοις ὕλη, ἀλλὰ τὸ ὑποκείμενον ἡ οὐσία. οἷον τί αἴτιον ἐκλείψεως, τίς ὕλη; οὐ γὰρ ἔστιν, ἀλλʼ ἡ σελήνη τὸ πάσχον. τί δʼ αἴτιον ὡς κινῆσαν καὶ φθεῖραν τὸ φῶς; ἡ γῆ. τὸ δʼ οὗ ἕνεκα ἴσως οὐκ ἔστιν. τὸ δʼ ὡς εἶδος ὁ λόγος, ἀλλὰ ἄδηλος ἐὰν μὴ μετὰ τῆς αἰτίας ᾖ ὁ λόγος. οἷον τί ἔκλειψις; στέρησις φωτός. ἐὰν δὲ προστεθῇ τὸ ὑπὸ γῆς ἐν μέσῳ γιγνομένης, ὁ σὺν τῷ αἰτίῳ λόγος οὗτος. ὕπνου δʼ ἄδηλον τί τὸ πρῶτον πάσχον. ἀλλʼ ὅτι τὸ ζῷον; ναί, ἀλλὰ τοῦτο κατὰ τί, καὶ τί πρῶτον; καρδία ἢ ἄλλο τι. εἶτα ὑπὸ τίνος; εἶτα τί τὸ πάθος, τὸ ἐκείνου καὶ μὴ τοῦ ὅλου; ὅτι ἀκινησία τοιαδί; ναί, ἀλλʼ αὕτη τῷ τί πάσχειν τὸ πρῶτον;
notes: "Natural substances that are eternal": the heavenly bodies, whose matter is only for motion in place (Book Λ, XII.2, 1069b24-26), the fifth body of On the Heavens (I.2-3). The Platonists, after Plato's Timaeus (40a-b), held them to be visible gods.

The eclipse is the model definition of the Posterior Analytics (II.2, 90a15-18; II.8, 93a29-b7): the account that includes the cause, "privation of light by the earth's coming between", says both what the eclipse is and why. Sleep is treated in On Sleep and Waking (2-3, 455b13-458a32), where the first part affected is the heart.

paragraphs.modern: Since some things are and are not without coming to be and perishing, like points, if they are, and the forms in general (for it is not the white that comes to be, but the wood comes to be white, if everything that comes to be comes to be from something and comes to be something), not all contraries could come to be from one another. A white man comes from a black man in one way, and white from black in another. Nor does everything have matter, but only those things that come to be and change into one another. Those that, without changing, are or are not, have no matter.
paragraphs.greek: ἐπεὶ δʼ ἔνια ἄνευ γενέσεως καὶ φθορᾶς ἔστι καὶ οὐκ ἔστιν, οἷον αἱ στιγμαί, εἴπερ εἰσί, καὶ ὅλως τὰ εἴδη (οὐ γὰρ τὸ λευκὸν γίγνεται ἀλλὰ τὸ ξύλον λευκόν, εἰ ἔκ τινος καὶ τὶ πᾶν τὸ γιγνόμενον γίγνεται), οὐ πάντα ἂν τἀναντία γίγνοιτο ἐξ ἀλλήλων, ἀλλʼ ἑτέρως λευκὸς ἄνθρωπος ἐκ μέλανος ἀνθρώπου καὶ λευκὸν ἐκ μέλανος· οὐδὲ παντὸς ὕλη ἔστιν ἀλλʼ ὅσων γένεσις ἔστι καὶ μεταβολὴ εἰς ἄλληλα· ὅσα δʼ ἄνευ τοῦ μεταβάλλειν ἔστιν ἢ μή, οὐκ ἔστι τούτων ὕλη.—

flags.taylor: in general forms and shapes
flags.why: The Greek says only "and the forms in general" (καὶ ὅλως τὰ εἴδη); Ross's "and shapes" is his own, to make plain that the forms here are the forms in things, the white, the shape, not the Platonic Forms. The modern version says "forms", in lower case.
